Gloomily Niels tried to wave the matter away. Erik nevertheless put a small padlock key, suspended from a wide ribbon, around his friend's neck. “Shall we go down?” he asked.

They set off. Beside the garden fence they found Frithjof lying down and eating green gooseberries, his eyes wet at the prospect of the farewell. He was hurt, too, because nobody had come to fetch him. Usually he needed no invitation, but this particular day seemed to call for some ceremony. Wordlessly he offered a handful of berries. The others, having eaten their favourite dishes at dinner, merely turned up their noses.
Erik gave a shudder. “They're sour!”

“That rubbish will give you indigestion!” Niels added, looking scornfully at the offered fruit. “How can you eat it? Throw it away and come to the deck-house.” His hands were in his pockets, so he indicated the key with his chin.
With that, the three boys went on together.

The deck-house was an old ship's cabin, painted green and bought years before at a beach auction. Set up beside the fjord, it had stored tools during construction of the dam, but now stood unused. The boys had claimed it for their ships, bows, arrows, jumping-poles, and other treasures. Especially precious were the forbidden necessities hidden there: gunpowder, tobacco, and matches.
With sombre ceremony Niels unlocked the deck-house. Inside, they felt about in the dark corners of the empty bunks until they located their belongings.
His head buried in a far corner, Erik announced, “I've decided I'm going to blow up my ship.”
“And mine, and Frithjof's!” Niels cried, making a grand gesture of dedication.
Frithjof protested, “Not mine, by Joe! What'll we have to sail once Erik's gone?”
“What indeed!” Niels echoed mockingly, turning his back in contempt.
Frithjof felt uneasy, but once the others were outside, he carefully shifted his boat into a safer hiding place.

Outside, they quickly packed the powder into the ships in nests of tarred oakum, raised the sails, fitted and lit the fuses, then jumped clear. Running beside them along the shore, they signalled to the imaginary crews. Each accidental change of course was loudly explained as proof of the captain's seamanship. But both vessels grounded at the point without exploding. Frithjof thus had the chance to offer up his cap's wadding nobly, so that new and better fuses could be made.

Under full sail the ships headed towards Sjaelland reef. Around them the Britisher's massive frigates lurched into a closed ring, white foam flying about their black bows, the forward guns filling the air with harsh thunder. Closer and closer came the _Albion_ and the _Conqueror_, their towering figure-heads brilliant in red and blue and glittering gold. Grey masses of canvas concealed the horizon. Huge white smoke-clouds rolled out and drifted low like a veil across the sunlit sparkle of the waves. Then a feeble little puff split the deck of Erik's ship. The oakum ignited; red fire burst out. Quick flames licked up the shrouds, ran along the spars, smouldered through the bolt-rope, and leapt like long lightning-streaks into the sails. Burning canvas shrank, tore, and flew seaward in large black flakes. High on the narrow summit of the schooner-mast the Danebrog still waved. Its staff burnt through, and the flag flapped like red wings impatient for battle. Then fire seized it too. Black with smoke, rudderless and without a helmsman, the dead, helpless ship drifted at the mercy of wind and breakers. Niels's ship burned less successfully. Its powder caught, some smoke appeared, and nothing more. That was not enough.
From the point Niels shouted, “Hey, there! Send her down! Turn the starboard cannon towards the aft hatch and fire a volley!” He stooped for a stone. “Ready, fire!” It flew from his hand.

Erik and Frithjof did the same, and soon the hull lay in pieces. They destroyed Erik's ship as well. Dragging the wreckage ashore, they heaped it with dry grass and seaweed to make a bonfire. Thick smoke rose from the burning pile, while crystals clinging to the weed popped and crackled in the fierce heat.

For a long while they sat silently around the fire. Then Niels, still sunk in gloom, suddenly stood and fetched everything he owned from the deck-house. He broke it all into fragments and fed it to the flames. Erik brought his possessions next; Frithjof contributed some of his too. The sacrificial blaze grew so tall that Erik feared it would be visible from the pasture and started smothering it with wet seaweed. Niels stood motionless, watching the smoke drift down the beach with sorrowful eyes. In the background Frithjof hummed a heroic song. Now and then, secretly, he accompanied it with a bard's sweeping gesture, as if stroking the strings of an unseen harp.

At last the fire dwindled. Erik and Frithjof turned homewards, leaving Niels to lock the deck-house. Afterwards he glanced cautiously at the departing boys, then flung key and ribbon far into the fjord. Erik happened to look back just then and saw them fall. Quickly he turned away again and challenged Frithjof to a race.
On the following day Erik departed.
For a time they missed him acutely and bitterly. Their lives had gradually come to depend on being shared by three. Three meant company, variety, change. Two meant boredom and no life at all.
What could two possibly find to occupy themselves with?
Could just two shoot at a target, or play ball? Friday and Robinson Crusoe were possible, certainly—but then who would play the savages?

Those Sundays! Niels grew so tired of living that he first revised his geography, then used Mr. Bigum's large atlas to push far beyond the required lessons. Eventually he began reading the entire Bible and keeping a diary. Frithjof, meanwhile, sank so low in his absolute loneliness that he sought comfort by playing with his sisters.

In time their memories lost some brightness and their longing its sharpest edge. On a quiet evening, the sun reddening the wall of the solitary room, the distant cuckoo's monotonous call might fade and leave the stillness wider and deeper. Then longing would steal into Niels and drain his strength. But it no longer tormented him. It lay vaguely and lightly upon him, half sweet, like pain already passing away.

His letters changed in the same way. At first they loosely strung together questions, wishes, and expressions of regret. Soon they lengthened, turned more towards outward events, and told stories. A polished style ran through them, hiding between the lines a conscious satisfaction in writing so well.

As the weeks went by, things that had not dared appear while Erik was there began raising their heads. Imagination scattered vivid flowers across the dull peace of an uneventful existence. Dreams wrapped Niels's mind in their atmosphere, carrying life's enticing fragrance. Concealed within that fragrance was the subtle poison of fantasies thirsty for life.

So Niels grows, while every influence of childhood works upon the yielding clay. Everything leaves a shape, everything matters: what happened and what was dreamed, what is known and what is only foreshadowed. Each lays a gentle but certain touch on that pattern of lines destined first to be carved deeper, then flattened and smoothed away.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: “Mrs. Boye—Mr. Lyhne. And Mr. Frithjof Petersen—Mrs. Boye.”

Erik made the introductions in Mikkelsen's studio, a bright, spacious room with a packed-clay floor and a ceiling twenty-five feet above it. Two large doorways at one end opened onto the yard; at the other, several doors led into smaller studios. Clay, plaster, and marble dust had turned everything grey. Overhead it thickened spiderweb threads until they resembled string; on the broad windowpanes it traced maps of rivers. It got into eyes, noses, and mouths. Along the shelves encircling the room, a jumble of casts displayed dust-outlined muscles, hair, and drapery, like a frieze depicting Jerusalem's destruction. Even the tall laurels in large tubs near one doorway were coated until they looked greyer than grey olive trees.

In the centre stood Erik at his modelling, a work blouse on his body and a paper cap over his dark, waving hair. A moustache had appeared, giving him a manly look beside the two friends who had just completed their bachelor's degrees. Still pale and worn from examinations, they looked properly provincial in clothes too new, with hair too closely clipped beneath rather oversized caps.

Not far from Erik's working platform, Mrs. Boye sat in a low chair with a tall back. One hand held an elaborately bound book, the other a piece of clay. She was small, very small, slightly brunette, with clear pale-brown eyes. Her skin glowed white, deepening in the shadows of her rounded cheek and neck to muted gold. This suited her glossy dark hair, which turned tawny blonde wherever the light struck it.

They arrived to find her laughing like a child: a long, joyful peal, merrily loud and wonderfully uninhibited. Her eyes too had a child's innocent directness. The open smile on her lips seemed younger still because a short upper lip left her mouth a little parted, revealing teeth white as milk.
Yet she was no child at all.

A little over thirty, perhaps? Neither the fullness beneath her chin nor her lower lip's ripe colour contradicted it. Her body was rounded, its firm, generous curves emphasized by a dark-blue dress, close-fitting as a riding-habit around waist, arms, and breast. A silk kerchief of muted crimson fell in ample folds round her shoulders and throat, its ends tucked inside her bodice's low, pointed neckline. Carnations of the same shade adorned her hair.
Glancing at the handsome book, Frithjof said, “I hope we haven't interrupted some enjoyable reading.”

“Not at all, not in the slightest. For the last hour we've been arguing over it,” Mrs. Boye answered. “When it comes to art, Mr. Refstrup is a thorough idealist. I find it all terribly tedious: crude reality must be purified, clarified, regenerated, and goodness knows what, until absolutely nothing remains. Just look at Mikkelsen's Bacchante, please—the one deaf Traffelini is carving in marble over there. Suppose I put her in a descriptive catalogue.... Good heavens! Number 77: A young lady in _negligé_ stands thoughtfully on both feet, wondering what to do with some grapes. I'd have her crush them—crush them until their red juice poured down her breast. Wouldn't that be better? Don't you agree?” In her eager, almost childish excitement, she caught Frithjof's sleeve and nearly shook him.
Frithjof conceded, “Yes, I do feel something is missing—a little freshness, perhaps—a certain spontaneity—”

“What's missing is simply naturalness. Good heavens, _why_ can't we be natural! Oh, I know the answer well enough: we haven't the courage. Artists and poets alike are too timid to acknowledge human nature as it actually is. But Shakespeare had the courage.”
From behind his model Erik observed, “You know, I've never really taken to Shakespeare. He rather overdoes things, I think. He spins you about until you've lost all sense of where you are.”

“I wouldn't go quite as far as that,” Frithjof objected, then added with a tolerant smile, “but equally I can't describe that great English poet's berserker frenzies as deliberate, intelligent artistic bravery.”

“Really? Goodness, how amusing you are!” She laughed heartily for so long that it tired her. Getting up, she wandered through the studio. Suddenly she turned towards Frithjof, opened her arms, and exclaimed, “God bless you!” Then she laughed again, almost folding herself in two.

Frithjof nearly took offence. But leaving in anger would be making too much fuss, particularly when he knew he was right; besides, the woman was very pretty. He remained and addressed Erik, carefully giving his voice an air of adult tolerance for Mrs. Boye to hear.
Mrs. Boye meanwhile drifted about the studio's far end, absently humming. At intervals the melody rose in a few swift, laughing trills, before falling back into slow and solemn recitative.
A bust of the young Augustus stood on a large packing-case. She started dusting it, then found clay and fashioned a moustache, a pointed beard, and finally earrings, attaching each to the head.

While she worked, Niels contrived to wander towards her, pretending to inspect the casts. She had not looked his way once, yet she must have noticed his presence. Without turning round, she extended a hand and asked him to fetch Erik's hat.
He placed the hat in her waiting hand, and she put it on Augustus's head.

Patting the disguised bust's cheek, she said, “Dear old Shakespeareson, foolish old man who never understood his own work! Was he just sitting there spilling ink when a Hamlet head appeared without his meaning it—was he?” She removed the hat and brushed his forehead with a motherly hand, as if smoothing back his hair. “Still, what a lucky fellow! More than half lucky, old poet boy!—You must at least admit he was a tolerable writer, this Shakespeare?”
A little irritated and blushing, Niels answered, “I admit to having an opinion of my own about the man.”
“Good gracious! Do you too have your own opinion of Shakespeare? Well, tell me what it is. Are you on our side or against us?” She posed beside the bust, smiling, an arm resting along its neck.

“I can't say whether this opinion, whose existence seems to surprise you, has the good fortune to gain importance by matching yours. But I believe I can call it _for_ you and your _protégé_. At least, I think he understood what he was doing, considered it carefully, and dared to do it. Often he dared despite doubt, and that doubt remains visible. Sometimes his courage went only halfway. Then he added details that blurred what he hadn't quite dared leave as he first conceived it.”
He continued speaking along these lines.

As he talked, Mrs. Boye became increasingly restless. Her eyes darted nervously first to one side and then the other, her fingers tapped impatiently, and a troubled expression clouded her face until it seemed positively painful.
Eventually she could restrain herself no longer.

“Please keep hold of your thought,” she burst out, “but Mr. Lyhne, I beg you to stop that hand movement, as if you were extracting teeth! Please, and don't let me put you off! There, now I'm listening perfectly, and I agree with you entirely.”
“Then there seems little point in my going on.”
“Why not?”
“If we're agreed?”
“If we're agreed!”

Neither intended anything particular by these final words. Yet they spoke as though delicate meanings filled them, exchanging subtle smiles like the fading gleam of a wit that had just passed between them. Each meanwhile wondered what the other meant, and felt faintly irritated at being too slow to grasp it.
They walked back to the far end of the studio, where Mrs. Boye settled again in her low chair.

Erik and Frithjof had talked themselves into a state of mutual boredom and welcomed their return. Frithjof came over to make himself pleasant to Mrs. Boye. Erik remained modestly in the background, as befitted their host.
Frithjof said, “If I were a curious person, I'd ask which book caused that argument with Refstrup just before we arrived.”
“Are you asking?”
“I am.”
“Ergo?”
Frithjof bowed in humble agreement. “Ergo!”

Holding the book aloft, she announced solemnly, “_Helge_—Oehlenschläger's _Helge_. Which canto? ‘The Mermaid visits King Helge.’ And which verse? The passage where Tangkjaer lies beside Helge, and he can no longer restrain his curiosity, so he turns
—_and at his side, With white arms soft and round, The greatest beauty he espied That e’er on earth was found._
_The maid had doffed her cloak of gray; Her lovely limbs were bare, Save for the robe like silver spray That veiled her form so fair._

That's the entire glimpse he grants us of the mermaid's beauty, and it's not enough for me. Here I want a rich, radiant picture, something so brilliant it leaves me breathless. I want to be admitted into the strange, mysterious beauty of a mermaid's body. What am I supposed to do with lovely limbs under a bit of gauze? Good heavens! She ought to be naked as a wave, surrounded by the sea's wild attraction. Her skin should carry something of a summer sea's phosphorescence, her hair something of the black, tangled terror of seaweed. Isn't that right? And a thousand watery colours should shift and glitter in her eyes. Her pale breast should have a sensual coolness; her limbs should flow like waves. Her kiss must hold the maelstrom's strength, and her embracing arms the yielding softness of foam.”
Her own words had set her glowing. Still alive with her subject, she stood regarding the young men with wide, questioning eyes like a child's.

No one said a word in answer. Niels had turned scarlet, and Erik looked intensely uncomfortable. Frithjof, entirely swept away, stared in frank admiration. Yet of the three he noticed least how captivatingly beautiful she was, standing within the enchantment her own words had made.

Within weeks, Niels and Frithjof called at Mrs. Boye's as regularly as Erik Refstrup. There, besides her pale niece, they encountered many young people: aspiring actors, poets, architects, and painters. They were artists more by reason of youth than ability, hopeful, brave, hungry for conflict, and quick to kindle with enthusiasm. A few were quiet dreamers, bleating yearningly towards yesterday's faded ideals. Most, however, overflowed with the ideas then considered modern. Modernity's theories intoxicated them, its energies drove them wild, its clear morning brilliance dazzled them. They were modern aggressively, modern extravagantly—perhaps especially because deep inside lay a strange instinctive yearning that had to be suppressed. The new spirit could not answer it, however universal, all-embracing, all-powerful, and all-illuminating that spirit claimed to be.

Even so, a storm's exhilaration filled their young souls. They believed in the light of thought's great stars, and their hope was deep as the ocean. Enthusiasm lifted them on eagle wings; their hearts swelled with the courage of thousands.

Life would doubtless wear this away in time, lull most of it to sleep. Worldly caution would destroy much, and cowardice would clear away whatever remained. But what did that matter? A time lived happily does not return in sorrow. Nothing the future brings can shrivel a day or erase an hour from the life already lived.

For Niels, the world was beginning to look different. Ten voices loudly announced the thoughts he had believed most secret and uncertain. His supposedly unique ideas had formed a mist-bound landscape, its outlines blurred, its depths unknown, its sounds subdued. Now that landscape stood uncovered in sharp, bright daylight, every detail plain, roads cut everywhere, people crowding along them. The very reality of what his imagination had created made it all seem strangely unreal.

He was no longer a solitary child-king ruling territories made by his dreams. He belonged to a crowd now, a man among troops, a soldier serving modern ideas. Someone had put a sword into his hand; ahead of him a banner flew.

What a marvellous, promising time! How strange to hear that vague, secret whisper of his soul ring through actual air: fierce, defiant trumpet calls, battering-rams thundering against temple walls, David's stone whistling at Goliath's forehead, triumphant fanfares. He seemed to hear himself speaking unfamiliar languages, with a clarity and force he did not possess, about what belonged to the deepest, most inward part of him.

The gospel of modernity, preaching dissolution and perfection, came from more than his contemporaries. Older men with respected names had also opened their eyes to the new ideas' splendour. Their language was grander, their conceptions more imposing. Names from earlier centuries followed in their wake. History stood beside them: world history, the history of human intelligence, thought's _Odyssey_. As young men they had felt the stirrings now exciting this generation and had testified to the spirit within. Then they had heard in their own voices that note which tells a speaker crying in the wilderness that he _is_ alone, and fallen silent. The young remembered only their speech, not their silence. They brought laurels and martyrs' crowns, eager to admire and happy in admiration. The honoured men did not reject this belated recognition. In good faith they accepted their crowns, saw themselves enlarged against history, and poetically removed the less heroic portions of their past. Their former convictions, cooled by hostile winds, soon glowed again as they talked.

Niels Lyhne's Copenhagen relatives, especially old Councillor Neergaard and his wife, thoroughly disliked his new circle. Modern ideas themselves were not the problem. Rather, some young men apparently considered long hair, enormous hunting-boots, and a little untidiness helpful to developing those ideas. Niels was no extremist in such matters, but seeing him with youths of that description was irritating, and having their friends encounter him so accompanied was worse. Yet all this counted for little beside his closeness to Mrs. Boye and his theatre outings with her and her pale niece.
Nothing definite could be alleged against Mrs. Boye, of course. But people talked. They had a great deal to say.

She came of good family, a Konneroy, one of the oldest and most distinguished patrician names in the city. Nevertheless, she had cut herself off from them. Some blamed the quarrel on a dissolute brother whom they had packed off to the colonies to be rid of him. The breach was certainly complete. There were even whispers that old Konneroy had cursed her and afterwards suffered a severe attack of his spring asthma.
This had all occurred after she was widowed.

Her husband, Mr. Boye, had been a pharmacist, an _assessor pharmacia_, and a knight. At his death he was sixty and possessed a barrel and a half of gold. As far as anyone knew, their marriage had been reasonably happy. During its first three years the older husband was deeply in love. Afterwards they pursued separate interests: he his garden and his reputation as an important man at gatherings of men, she the theatre, romantic music, and German poetry.
Then he died.

After a year's mourning, the widow travelled to Italy for two or three years, mostly spent in Rome. Stories that she smoked opium at the French club were untrue, as was the claim that she had posed for a sculpture like Paulina Borghese. The little Russian prince who killed himself while she was in Naples had not done so on her account. German artists did, however, serenade her endlessly. And one morning she really had dressed as an Albanian peasant girl and sat on church steps high in the Via Sistina. A newly arrived painter had hired her to pose, a pitcher on her head and a small brown boy beside her holding her hand. At any rate, a painting showing exactly that hung on her wall.

Returning from Italy, she met a fellow countryman, a celebrated and intelligent critic who would have preferred being a poet. People called him negative and sceptical, keen-minded, pitiless and harsh towards others because he treated himself just as harshly, believing this excused his brutality. Yet he was not quite the man they imagined. He was less repulsively unyielding, less sturdily consistent than he appeared. He constantly opposed the age's idealist tendencies and used disparaging names for them. Still, those dreamy, airy ideals attracted him: the intensely blue mysticism, the inaccessible heights, the lights that vanished as you watched. They appealed more strongly than the earthbound views he defended and, most of the time, believed.

Almost against his wishes, he fell in love with Mrs. Boye. He kept silent, for his love was neither youthful and open nor hopeful. To him she belonged to another race, finer and happier than his own. His love carried resentment, an instinctive fury against every sign of that finer breeding in her.

He examined her feelings, tastes, convictions, and outlook with jealous hostility. Every weapon he had—subtle eloquence, merciless reasoning, harsh authority, ridicule disguised as pity—was used to win her to his position. He succeeded. But once truth had triumphed and she resembled him, he discovered he had won too completely. He had loved her former self, her illusions and prejudices, her mistakes and dreams, not the person she had become. Disgusted with her, himself, and everything in his native country, he left and never returned. Just then, however, she had begun to love him.

Naturally this attachment supplied abundant material for gossip, and people made all they could of it. The Councillor's wife related the story to Niels in the tone elderly virtue adopts towards youthful transgression. His reaction both offended and appalled the old lady. He answered loftily about society's tyranny and personal freedom, the mob's vulgar respectability and the nobility of passion.
After that, he seldom visited his concerned relatives. Mrs. Boye, on the other hand, saw him more often than ever.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: It was a spring evening. As the sun sank towards the horizon, it cast red light into the room. The windmill's sails on the embankment swept shadows over walls and windowpanes, passing and returning with monotonous regularity: one moment dark, two moments bright.

Niels Lyhne sat at the window, looking through the embankment's dark, glossy elms towards the burning clouds. He had spent the day in the country, walking beneath flowering beeches, beside green rye-fields, and across meadows bright with flowers. Everything had seemed so light and lovely: the blue sky, the shining Sound, the astonishing beauty of the women he passed. He had sung along the woodland path. Gradually the song lost its words, then its rhythm, then its sound, until a dizzying silence overtook him. Even with his eyes closed he felt his body drinking the light and his nerves quivering in response. Each breath of cool, heady air sent blood racing more fiercely through his trembling, helpless veins. He seemed filled with spring's swarming forces of growth and budding and germination, mysteriously seeking release through him in one enormous cry. He thirsted for that cry and listened for it until listening became a vague, swollen longing.
Sitting now beside the window, he felt that same longing stirring to life again.

He yearned for a thousand shivering dreams, cool and delicate images, translucent colours, vanishing perfumes, exquisite music streaming from silvery strings stretched taut and high. Then silence: its very heart, where no wandering note had ever travelled upon the air, where everything rested as if dead, bathed in the quiet glow of reds and the languorous warmth of burning perfume.—No, this was not what he wanted. But the images drifted out of his mood and drowned everything else until he turned away and resumed his own line of thought.

He was tired of himself, of chilly ideas and dreams made in the brain. Life a poem? Not if you spent it endlessly making poetry out of your own life instead of living. How harmless it all was, and empty, empty, empty! Chasing yourself, slyly tracking your own footprints, inevitably round in circles. Pretending to plunge into life's current while remaining on the bank fishing for yourself, hauling yourself out in one peculiar disguise after another! If only something could overwhelm him—life, passion, love—so that instead of shaping it into poems, he had to let it shape him!

Without thinking, he raised a hand as though to fend it off. Deep down he was frightened of that immense thing, passion: a gale sweeping away everything established, sanctioned, and acquired in humanity like a heap of dead leaves. He did not welcome it! A roaring fire consuming itself in its own smoke—no, _he_ preferred to burn slowly.

Yet continuing at half speed through quiet water, land always visible, seemed so insignificant. If only the waves and storm would arrive! If he knew how, he would hoist his sails to the yards and make a glorious run across life's Spanish Main! Farewell to days dripping slowly past, farewell to pleasant little hours! Peace to you, dull moods that must be polished with poetry to give a shine, lukewarm feelings that freeze even when dressed in warm dreams! Go where you belong! I am sailing towards a shore where emotions coil like rich vines around every fibre of the heart, a luxuriant forest: for each vine dying, twenty flowering; for each in flower, a hundred still in bud.
Oh, if only I were already there!

The longing exhausted him; he grew disgusted with himself. He needed company. But naturally Erik was out, Frithjof had spent the whole morning with him, and the theatre was no longer an option at this hour. Still, he left and wandered dispiritedly through the streets.
Perhaps Mrs. Boye was at home. It wasn't one of her receiving evenings, and the hour was rather late. Still, why not try?

She was home, and alone. The spring air had tired her too much to accompany her niece to a dinner party. Instead she had chosen the sofa, strong tea, and Heine. Now poetry had wearied her, and she wanted a game of lotto.
So they sat playing lotto. Fifteen, twenty, thirty-seven: number followed number, dice rattled in a bag, and from upstairs came the irritating rumble of balls across the floor....
After a long spell without covering any numbers, Mrs. Boye said, “This isn't entertaining. Is it? No!” She answered herself, shaking her head sadly. “But what other game is there?”
Folding her hands on the counters before her, she looked at Niels with a helpless question in her eyes.
Niels could think of nothing.

“Anything except music!” She lowered her face to her hands and kissed each knuckle in turn, along the entire row and then all the way back. Looking up, she said, “What a wretched existence this is. Adventures simply aren't possible, and surely life's tiny incidents can't be enough to keep us cheerful. Don't you feel it as well?”

“My best suggestion is that we copy the Caliph in the Arabian Nights. You're already wearing a silk kimono. Wrap a white cloth round your head, lend me that big Indian shawl, and we'd easily pass for a pair of merchants from Mossul.”
“And what would these two unlucky merchants find to do?”
“Walk down to Storm Bridge, pay twenty pieces of gold for a boat, and sail up the dark river.”
“Beyond the sand-chests?”
“Yes, with coloured lanterns at the masthead.”

“Like Ganem, the Slave of Love.—Oh, I know that sort of thinking so well! It's just like a man, fussing over scenery and background until the setting makes him forget the action. Haven't you noticed how much less women live in their imagination? We can't savour pleasure in advance by imagining it, or flee pain through imaginary consolations. What exists, exists. Imagination is so harmless. Sometimes, once we're as old as I am, we settle for its impoverished little comedy. But we never ought to—never!”
She sank languidly back along the sofa, chin supported by her hand, elbow resting in the cushions. Her dreamy gaze travelled nowhere in particular; she seemed absorbed in sorrowful thoughts.

Niels too said nothing. In the still room every restless hop of the canary was audible. The great clock ticked through the silence, seeming louder and louder. Suddenly a string in the open piano stirred and released a long, faint, fading note, which mingled with the stillness's gentle singing.

Under the lamp's soft yellow glow, which bathed her from head to foot, she looked very young. The contrast was alluring: a beautiful, powerfully shaped throat and a matron's Charlotte Corday cap, paired with candid childish eyes and the small mouth parted over milk-white teeth.
Niels watched her with admiration.

“How strange, to miss oneself!” she said. “Yet so often, so very often, I miss the girl I used to be. I love her as someone close to me, someone with whom I shared happiness and life and everything, then lost without being able to prevent it. What an extraordinary time that was! You can't imagine the purity and tenderness of a girl's soul when love first begins. Only music can express it. Picture a celebration in a fairy palace, the air bright as blushing silver, filled with cool flowers whose colours slowly alter. Everything is song, joyful but gentle. Uncertain intimations glow like enchanted wine in delicate dream-cups. Song and perfume everywhere, a thousand fragrances floating through the rooms. Oh, thinking of it makes me want to cry. And to think that, if some miracle returned it exactly as it was, it couldn't support me now. I'd fall straight through, like a cow attempting to dance on cobwebs.”
“No, the opposite,” Niels said eagerly. His voice trembled as he continued: “The love you're capable of now would be far finer, much more spiritual than the love of that young girl.”

“Spiritual! I detest that spiritual kind of love. Its flowers are cotton fabric; they don't even grow. They're taken out of the head and planted in the heart because the heart grows none itself. That's precisely what I envy the girl for: she is real all through. She doesn't fill love's cup with imagination as a substitute. Her love may be threaded and overshadowed by imagined scenes, picture after picture in a vast, teeming uncertainty. Don't suppose she therefore values them more than the ground she stands on. It is simply that every sense, instinct, and power in her reaches everywhere for love, everywhere, without tiring. She doesn't feast on fantasies or even settle into them. She is much more genuine than that—so genuine that, without knowing it, she often becomes innocently cynical. You can't conceive, for example, the intoxicating pleasure a girl gets from secretly breathing the cigar-smell in her lover's clothes. A whole blaze of fancy means a thousand times less. I despise imagination. When our entire being longs towards another's heart, what use is being admitted only to the cold anteroom of his imagination! Yet that happens constantly. How often must we allow the man we love to dress us in his fancies, set a halo over our head, fasten wings to our shoulders, and wrap us in a star-covered robe! Only then, disguised like that, does he decide we're worthy of love. But dressed up so extravagantly we can't be ourselves. Men bewilder us by kneeling and worshipping in the dust, instead of simply accepting and loving what we are.”

Niels was quite bewildered by her words. He had retrieved her fallen handkerchief and sat breathing its heady perfume. Absorbed in examining her hand, he was entirely unprepared for the impatient question in her look. Still, he managed to say that a man could give no finer proof of love: needing to justify to himself such inexpressible devotion to a human being, he raised her high and surrounded her with a halo of divinity.
Mrs. Boye replied, “That's exactly what I find offensive—as though we weren't sufficiently divine as we are.”
Niels gave a self-satisfied smile.

“Don't smile. I'm not making a joke. It's a very serious matter, because beneath all this worship lies a fanatical tyranny. It squeezes us into the shape of man's ideal. Cut off a heel, trim away a toe! Whatever doesn't fit his idea must go. Perhaps no force is used; instead it is ignored, methodically forgotten, denied every chance to develop. Meanwhile qualities we lack, or that scarcely belong to us, are encouraged into the rankest growth. They're praised extravagantly, assumed to exist in us to perfection, and made the foundation of his love. We are being drilled, I tell you. A man's love puts us through a drill. And we obey. Even women who love nobody obey, the despicable little servants we are!”
She sat up from her reclining position and fixed Niels with a threatening look.

“If I were beautiful! I mean irresistibly beautiful, more alluring than any woman ever born, so that everyone who saw me fell under a spell of agonizing, unquenchable love—then I'd use that beauty to force them to worship _me_. Not some inherited, bloodless ideal, but myself as I am, every inch and outline of _my_ being, every spark of _my_ nature!”

Now she stood at her full height. Niels felt he should leave, but lingered, turning daring phrases over in his mind without finding courage to speak them. Finally, gathering all his boldness, he took her hand and kissed it. She offered the other hand for a kiss too. After that he could manage nothing more than “Good-night.”
Niels Lyhne was in love with Mrs. Boye, and being in love made him happy.

Walking home through the very streets he had wandered so miserably earlier that evening, he felt ages had passed since then. A new balance, a serious dignity, had entered his bearing. He carefully fastened his gloves with an unspoken sense that he had undergone some great transformation, one which somehow required him to fasten those gloves—carefully.
Thoughts absorbed him too deeply for sleep, so he climbed up onto the embankment.

His thoughts seemed to move with extraordinary quietness. The calm surprised him, and he did not entirely trust it. Deep within himself he sensed a soft but persistent bubbling: something welling, seething, pushing forward, yet far, far off. He felt as if waiting for a thing that must travel a great distance, for remote music approaching little by little—singing, murmuring, foaming, rushing, roaring, then swirling down upon him. It would sweep him up somehow, carry him somewhere he could not imagine, surge in like a flood, break like surf, and then—
For now, though, he remained calm. Only a faint, trembling song sounded far away; otherwise everything was peaceful and still.

He loved. Over and over he said the words aloud. They sounded strangely dignified and held profound meanings. He was no longer imprisoned in childhood's imaginary realm, no longer tossed about by purposeless desires and cloudy dreams. He had escaped the elf-land that had grown alongside and around him, clasping him in a hundred arms, covering his eyes with a hundred hands. Breaking free, he had become his own master. It still reached for him, pleaded with voiceless eyes, beckoned in fluttering white robes, but its power was gone, like a dream slain by daylight or mist dispersed by sunshine. Wasn't his young love daylight, sunshine, the whole world? Until now he had paraded in royal purple not yet woven, occupied a throne not yet built. Now he stood on a mountain looking over the world spread like a plain below. That world thirsted for song, yet he did not exist for it and nobody even expected him. What joy to think that across that silent, wakeful immensity, no breath of his spirit had yet moved a leaf or stirred a ripple. It all remained to be won, and he knew he could win it. Such invincible strength belongs only to those whose songs remain unsung, beating within their own breasts.

Fragrance filled the mild spring air without saturating it as on summer nights. It seemed instead to run in streaks: the sharp resin-scent of young poplars, the cool breath of late violets, the sweet almond perfume of cherry-trees. The scents approached, mingled, drifted away, dissolved. Sometimes one sprang free of the others, only to die at once or fade slowly on a breeze. Light moods crossed his mind like shadows of that uncertain dance. The perfumes teased his senses by appearing and disappearing as they pleased; so his mind was frustrated in its wish to rise and rest in easy flight on a mood's gently moving wings. His moods were not yet birds strong enough to carry him. They were only feathers and down, blown by the wind, falling like snow and melting away.

He tried to summon the image of her talking as she lay on the sofa, but could not. Instead he saw her disappearing down a tree-lined lane; sitting with her hat on, reading, gloved fingers holding a large white page just before turning it, then turning page after page. He saw her getting into the carriage after an evening at the theatre and nodding through the glass. The carriage moved off and he watched. It kept moving, and still his eyes followed. Unimportant faces spoke to him; people unseen for years passed down the street and turned to look back. Still the carriage drove on. He could not dismiss it, could picture nothing else because it kept intervening. Then, just as impatience made him nervous, the right image arrived: yellow lamplight, eyes, mouth, the hand supporting her chin, everything as vivid as if present before him in the dark.

How beautiful she was, how gentle, how fair! His desire knelt at her feet, begging for all that seductive loveliness. Come down from your throne to me! Become my slave! Fasten the chain round your own neck, but not as a game—I mean to pull it, to see submission in every limb and bondage in your eyes! Oh, if I could bring you to me with a love-philtre. But no: a love-philtre would force you, and you would surrender without choosing. I want no master over you except myself. Break your will with your own hands and offer it humbly to me. You shall be queen and I your slave, but this slave's foot must rest upon your queenly neck. The desire is not madness. Isn't a woman's love by nature proud and strong, and willing to bend? To be weak and reign—that, I know, is love.

He felt he would never reach the part of her soul united with her beauty's rich, glowing, sensuous softness. It would never enfold him in those shining Juno arms, never offer that lovely neck to his kisses in passionate surrender—not in all eternity. He understood it clearly. The young girl within her he could win, perhaps had won already. He was sure that this full-blooded beauty felt her dead maiden self mysteriously waking inside its living grave, ready to embrace him with slender arms and meet him with shy young lips. But that was not the love he felt. He loved exactly what he could not possess in her: that neck, its warm flower-white skin shining with golden dew beneath the dark hair. He sobbed with passionate longing and twisted his hands in powerless desire. Throwing his arms around a tree, he pressed his cheek to the bark and wept.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Niels Lyhne had a habit of reflection that hobbled him. It sprang from an instinctive retreat from decisive acts, and behind that instinct lay an unacknowledged feeling that he had no personality. He fought this reflective habit continually, sometimes lashing himself with ugly names for it, sometimes dressing it up as a virtue rooted in his deepest being and inseparable from all his powers and prospects. Yet whatever he called it, from whatever side he considered it, he hated it as a hidden disability. He might conceal it from everyone else, but could never conceal it from himself; whenever he was alone, it was there to shame him. How he envied the boldness that flings itself confidently into speech, without considering that speech entails actions and actions entail consequences, until the consequences come running after it. Those who had that boldness looked to him like centaurs, horse and man poured into one mould. For them the urge and the leap were a single thing; he, meanwhile, remained horse and rider separately, with the impulse here and the leap somewhere quite different.

Whenever he imagined telling Mrs. Boye that he loved her—and everything had to be imagined beforehand—he saw himself distinctly in the scene: his posture, each movement, his entire body viewed from behind, in profile, and face-on. He watched himself hesitate in that fever of indecision which scattered his wits and left him helpless. There he would stand, waiting for her reply as though it must be a stroke that brought him to his knees, when it might instead be a shuttlecock, something he could send back a hundred different ways and receive again in a hundred others.

He considered telling her aloud; he considered putting it in a letter; but he could never just let the words come out. He expressed it only through disguised avowals and a partly acted lyrical ardour, pretending to be swept into burning speeches and extravagant hopes. Still, a peculiar intimacy began to form between them, made from a young man's reverent love, a dreamer's passionate yearning, and a woman's delight in being the unattainable goal of romantic desire. Their attachment assumed the shape of a myth; neither could have said how it arose, this quiet, colourless myth born in a drawing-room. The central figure was a beautiful woman who, when very young, had loved a great man of the intellect. He had left her and died abroad, abandoned and forgotten. Through long years the beautiful woman mourned him, though nobody knew her pain; only solitude was holy enough to witness her sorrow. At last a young man appeared, who revered the dead thinker as his master, who breathed his spirit and burned with enthusiasm for his work. This young man loved the grieving woman. She felt her happy days, long buried, rise out of their grave into life. A strange, delicious confusion possessed her. The present and the past dissolved together in the silver haze of a dim, dreamlike day, where she loved the young man partly for himself and partly as another man's likeness, and surrendered half her soul to him. He, however, must move cautiously, or the bubble of the dream would break. He must keep a firm barrier against every burning, earthly desire, or he would drive away that gentle twilight and awaken her again to grief.

Under the protection of this myth, their intimacy slowly settled into an established shape. Alone together they used their first names, becoming Niels and Tema, and the niece's appearances were kept as brief as possible. Niels did sometimes attempt to cross the agreed boundaries, certainly; but Mrs. Boye had so much more power that she could put down these little rebellions with effortless gentleness. He had to yield, and content himself for another while with an imaginary passion acted out in real tableaux. Their attachment never dwindled into a dull platonic affair, nor subsided into the sleepy sameness of custom. Sleep or rest had very little to do with it. Niels Lyhne never exhausted his hope. Whenever it blazed into a demand, she softly smothered it, but that only sent it burning more fiercely underground. And with what endless flirtations Mrs. Boye stoked the fire, with her disarming frankness and her fearless freedom in speaking of the most intimate matters! Nor did she control every move in this game. At times, in her idle blood, she dreamed of rewarding his imperfectly subdued devotion with all the ecstasy love could give, so that she might enjoy his astonished bliss. Such a dream did not readily fade. When Niels next appeared, she would receive him with the uneasiness of someone aware of sin, the timid air of a guilty woman, a delicious embarrassment that set a strange vibration of passion in the air.

Something else, too, kept a tension alive between them. There was enough manly strength in Niels Lyhne's love to make him chivalrously refuse to seize in fantasy what actual life withheld. Even in that private realm where everything obeyed his wishes, he treated Mrs. Boye with the respect he would have shown if she were truly there.

Their attachment thus had solid supports on either side, with no prospect of its immediate collapse. Indeed, it might have been devised for someone of Niels Lyhne's temperament, so reflective and yet so thirsty for life. A game it might be, but its pieces were real, and it supplied all the hidden current of passion that he required.

Niels Lyhne had resolved to become a poet, and many of the outward conditions of his life encouraged his mind that way and roused the abilities the work demanded. As yet, though, his dreams were almost his only subject, and nothing is more repetitive or more monotonous than imagination. That country of dreams looks limitless and endlessly various; in reality it contains only a handful of short, well-trodden tracks, along which everyone travels without ever stepping aside. Individuals differ from one another, but their dreams do not. In dreams they invariably secure the three or four things they want, more swiftly or slowly, more fully or less fully, but in the end they secure them. Nobody seriously pictures himself coming away empty-handed. Consequently, nobody discovers who he is in his dreams, or learns from them the particular character of his own being. Dreams do not tell us what satisfaction we find in the treasure once won, how we surrender it when it is lost, what enjoyment we draw from possessing it, or where we go when it is snatched away.

Until now, Niels Lyhne's poems had merely voiced an aesthetic personality that held, in a general sort of way, that spring was abundant, the sea immense, love sensual, and death sad. The poems contained nothing of himself; he was only the person who arranged the lines. This now began to change. He was courting a woman, and he wanted her to love him: Niels Lyhne from Lönborggaard, aged twenty-three, with a slight stoop, fine hands, little ears, and a somewhat shy disposition. It was this man he wanted loved, rather than the splendid Nicolaus of his fantasies, a slightly older man with a commanding posture and an assured manner. So he began to feel a living interest in this Niels, whose company he had previously endured as one puts up with a friend who is not quite fit to introduce. He had spent so much time adorning himself with virtues he did not own that he had never paused to notice those he did. Now he started assembling his own character out of fragments of childhood recollection and impression, and the most intensely remembered moments of his life. With delighted surprise he watched the pieces join and fuse, little by little, into a personality far more intimately known than the one he had pursued in fancy. This person was infinitely more real, stronger, and more richly gifted. Here was no lifeless remnant of an ideal, but a living being through which innumerable changing possibilities moved, giving it a unity of a thousand forms. Good God, he _did_ have gifts that were useful exactly as they were! He _was_ Aladdin: everything he had besieged the heavens to obtain had already dropped straight into his turban.

A joyful season followed for Niels: that magnificent season when the strong current of growth bears us triumphantly over the stagnant places in our character. Strength swells inside us until we feel ready to set our shoulders against mountains, if necessary, and boldly continue building our Tower of Babel. We mean it to thrust through heaven; it ends as a low, squat building, to which we spend the rest of our lives making additions, a hesitant little spire today, an eccentric projecting window tomorrow.

All was different now. His character, his gifts, and his work meshed like the teeth of interlocking wheels. Pausing to admire his art never occurred to him. As soon as he finished something he threw it aside, having already grown beyond it in the course of making it. It was only another stair towards a goal that kept withdrawing, one among many stairs on a road already behind him, forgotten even as the sound of his steps still rang along it.

New desires and thoughts carried him towards greater strength and a wider view, and in the process he became steadily more alone. His former companions dropped away one after another and disappeared from sight. They ceased to interest him as the distinction grew fainter between these professed rebels and the majority they assailed. Everything seemed to run together into a vast, hostile bulk of tediousness. What, after all, did they produce when they sounded the charge? Gloomy poems announcing that dogs frequently showed more loyalty than people, and convicts more honesty than men at liberty; sonorous odes explaining that green forests and brown heath were better than dusty towns; tales contrasting peasants' goodness with wealthy men's wickedness, vigorous nature with bloodless civilization, old people's cramped outlook with youth's divine entitlement. How little they asked for once they put pen to paper! At least in conversation, safely enclosed by four walls, they dared rather more.
When his own moment arrived, he would give them something to hear: a trumpet sounding the advance!

His earlier friendships also began to suffer, above all his friendship with Frithjof. Frithjof had a decisive temperament, a head well suited to systems, and shoulders broad enough to carry dogmas. He had, in fact, read rather too much Heiberg and swallowed the whole as revealed truth. It never occurred to him that system-builders were ingenious people who constructed their systems out of their books, instead of constructing books out of systems. Young people who pledge allegiance to a system notoriously become formidable dogmatists, thanks to youth's often admirable fondness for things complete and bounded. Besides, once the entire truth belongs to you, keeping it to yourself would be inexcusable. Surely you cannot leave your less fortunate neighbours to wander down their mistaken paths. You must guide and educate them, cut back their straying shoots with affectionate firmness, press them against the wall with considerate force, and show them the prescribed lines of growth. Then one day, shaped into properly trained and artistically arranged espaliers, they will thank you for your pains, even if their gratitude comes rather late.

Niels liked to announce that nothing pleased him more than criticism; in reality he liked admiration better. Criticism from Frithjof was especially intolerable. He had always considered Frithjof his dependent, and Frithjof had always been happy enough to put on the uniform of Niels's principles and beliefs. Yet now he proposed to act as an equal, parading about in a cloak he had chosen himself! Naturally he had to be put in his place. Niels began with an air of genial superiority, trying to make Frithjof see himself as ridiculous. When this failed, he resorted to outrageous paradoxes which he contemptuously refused to argue about. He simply flung them down in their grotesque ugliness and withdrew into a silence designed to irritate.
That was how the distance between them widened.

Things went better between him and Erik. Even as boys, their friendship had maintained a little distance, a sort of modesty of the spirit. This had protected it from the excessive familiarity that so readily endangers friendship. They had shared enthusiasms in their souls' banqueting hall and talked confidentially in the drawing-room, but neither had presumed to wander into the other's bedrooms, bathrooms, or the other private chambers of that inward house.

That was still true. If anything, their reserve had increased, particularly on Niels's side; yet it did not diminish their friendship. Its foundation remained what it had always been: Niels Lyhne's admiration for Erik's lively courage and daring, his apparent ease with life, his promptness in reaching out and taking hold. Nevertheless, Niels could not disguise from himself how unequal the friendship was. Erik certainly did not lack genuine love for him or confidence in him; quite the reverse. Nobody esteemed Niels more highly. Erik thought him so immeasurably above himself in intellectual matters that criticism never entered his head. But this unquestioning reverence made him set Niels, his activities, and his interests far outside the horizon visible to himself. He felt certain Niels would travel a long way on his chosen road; he felt just as certain that his own feet had no business there, and never even tried to follow.

This seemed rather unfair to Niels. Erik's ideals were not his own, and the romanticism, or romantic sentimentality, that Erik sought to embody in his art was foreign to his convictions. Yet Niels could summon a more generous sympathy, enabling him to keep faithful track of his friend's progress, to celebrate every advance with him, and to sustain his hope when he made no headway.

Such was the inequality in their friendship. It was hardly surprising that Niels became aware of what was missing just when his own mind was wrestling with unfamiliar ideas and he needed someone sympathetic into whose ears he could pour his thoughts. The discovery embittered him. He began to inspect more critically the friend he had always treated with such indulgence. A bleak loneliness settled over him as he saw everything brought from home and the old days slipping away, leaving him to make his way abandoned and unremembered. The door into his past was bolted; he stood on the threshold alone, with nothing in his hands. Whatever he wanted, whatever he required, he would have to obtain by his own efforts: other friends, another refuge, fresh affections, and fresh memories.
For over a year Mrs. Boye had been the sole person who truly shared Niels's life. Then his mother wrote that his father was gravely ill, and her letter summoned him home to Lönborggaard.
His father had died before he reached home.

Niels felt almost criminal when he remembered how little he had missed his home during the past several years. His mind had visited it often, certainly, but always as a traveller, carrying other countries' dust on his clothing and other places' recollections in his heart. He had never ached for it with fierce homesickness, as the lovely refuge of his existence; he had never yearned to kiss its ground or lie beneath its roof. He now regretted that disloyalty to his home. Under the weight of grief, his regret deepened into a dim sense of complicity, as if his faithlessness had somehow opened the door to death. How had he ever been happy living away from a place that drew him now with such mysterious force? Every part of him clung to it in a boundless, desolate yearning. He was restless because he could not unite himself with it as completely as he wished; miserable because the innumerable memories calling to him from every bush and corner, from noises and countless smells, from shifting light and even from silence, all spoke from so far away. He could not seize them in the full intensity he longed for. They only murmured within him, like the rustle of leaves descending to earth, or the little splash of water passing onward, always onward....

Fortunate in grief is anyone who, losing a beloved person, can spend every tear on vacancy, desolation, and solitude alone. Far more painful and bitter are the tears offered in payment for the past, when you withheld love from someone now gone, someone to whom you can never repair the wrong. Everything returns then. The cruel words return, the answers delicately tainted with poison, the merciless condemnation, the senseless rage; and so do the unspoken unkindnesses, the swift judgments that only crossed your mind, the unnoticed shrug, the concealed smile of impatience and contempt. They fly back like spiteful arrows and drive their barbs deep into your breast. Their barbs are blunt: their sharp points have broken off in the heart that no longer lives. You can put nothing right now, nothing at all. Love fills your heart at last, when at last it is too late. Take that overflowing heart to the cold grave! Does it close the distance? Set flowers there, weave wreaths: will either bring relief?

Wreaths were being woven at Lönborggaard. There, too, people remembered with anguish the moments when rougher voices had drowned out love. There, too, the grave's tightly closed mouth, with its severe lines, seemed to speak to them of remorse.

The time was shadowed and sorrowful, yet one brightness lay within it: mother and son drew nearer than they had been in many long years. For all their deep affection, they had always kept a kind of watch on each other. A restraint had entered their dealings from the day Niels became too big for his mother's lap. Her nervous excitability had made him draw back, while his hesitations and shyness had seemed to her something foreign. Now life itself, which raises the pitch and lowers it and brings things into harmony, had made their hearts ready. Soon it would let them belong entirely to one another.

Less than two months after the burial, Mrs. Lyhne became desperately ill, and for many days her survival remained doubtful. The worry of those weeks pushed their previous sorrow aside. By the time she began to mend, both she and Niels felt as though years had intervened between themselves and that newly dug grave. To Mrs. Lyhne especially, the interval seemed immense. During her illness she had believed she would die, and death had terrified her. Now recovery had started and the doctor pronounced her out of danger; even so, she could not shake off the dark thoughts that possessed her.

Her recovery was dispiriting. Strength seemed to trickle back unwillingly, a drop at a time. Instead of the soft, restorative sleepiness of healing, she felt an agitated weariness, a crushing awareness of weakness, and a continual, helpless craving to be strong again.

Eventually this altered. She improved more quickly and regained her strength. But the belief that she must soon leave life remained. It cast a shadow across her, holding her imprisoned in a melancholy full of longing and unease.

One evening she sat by herself in the summer sitting-room, looking through the doors, which stood wide open. The garden trees screened the sunset's crimson and gold. At one point, though, a gap between the trunks exposed a patch of flaming sky. From it long shafts of rich golden sunlight spread outward, bringing out green colours and brown-bronze gleams in the dark masses of leaves.

Far over the tossing treetops, clouds moved like dark shapes across the smoky red heavens. In their haste they shed small wisps behind them, slender scraps of cloud that the sun saturated with the glow of wine.

Mrs. Lyhne listened to the wind moving in the branches. Her head stirred almost imperceptibly to the irregular rise and fall of each gust, as it rushed towards her, swept noisily through, and faded. Her gaze, however, was distant, farther away even than the clouds before her eyes. Dressed in her widow's black, she sat pale, with a touching look of uneasiness around her barely pink lips. Her fingers kept playing with the small, thick volume in her lap: Rousseau's _Héloïse_. More books lay stacked about her, Schiller, Staffeldt, Evald, and Novalis, together with broad portfolios of engravings showing ancient churches, ruined buildings, and lakes among mountains.

Doors began to open and close. Footsteps followed, apparently searching the rooms farther inside for someone; a moment later Niels entered. He had taken a long walk beside the fjord. The outdoor air had reddened his cheeks, and his hair still showed the wind's disorder.
Outdoors, blue-grey shades had taken possession of the heavens. A handful of large raindrops struck the window glass.

Niels described the great waves rolling ashore and the seaweed they had thrown onto the beach, then spoke of the people he had encountered and the things he had noticed. While telling her, he collected the books, shut the garden doors, and secured the windows. Finally he settled onto the little stool beside his mother's feet, held her hand, and rested his face against her knee.
Outside it was almost pitch-dark now. Rain rattled down like hailstones, streaming across the window frames and glass.

After a long quiet pause Niels said, “Can you remember how we used to sit this way at twilight, setting off to find adventures? Father would be in his office discussing things with Jens Overseer, and we could hear Duysen clattering the tea things in the dining-room. When they brought the lamp, both of us would come back from our extraordinary adventures into the safe warmth of the room. But I remember perfectly how I always believed the tale continued after we stopped, carrying on somewhere underneath the hills along the Ringkjöbing road.”
He could not see the longing in his mother's smile, but he felt the soft movement of her hand across his hair.
A little later she asked, “Can you remember all those promises you made, that once you were grown you would sail away in a great ship and come home with every treasure in the world for me?”

“How could I forget! There were to be hyacinths, because you were so fond of them, and a palm to replace the one that died, and gold and marble pillars. Your stories were always full of pillars, so many of them. Do you remember those?”

“I've waited for that ship. No, darling, don't move; you haven't understood. I wasn't waiting for gifts for myself: I meant the ship that would carry your destiny.... I wanted you to have a splendid, full life, to walk along radiant roads.... Renown, everything. No, I don't mean that, only that you should join the people who struggle for the highest things. I can't explain it, but ordinary happiness and ordinary ambitions make me so weary. Can you understand?”

“You wanted a Sunday child for your son, dear mother: someone who doesn't have to share the common harness, someone with a heaven of his own for his salvation and a private hell for his damnation as well. We were going to carry flowers in our ship, weren't we? Wonderful flowers to scatter across a dreary world. Only the ship never arrived, and a sorry pair of birds they were, Niels and his mother, weren't they?”
“Darling, have I wounded you? They were only dreams, after all; don't let them trouble you!”

For a long while Niels said nothing, embarrassed by the words he wanted to speak. At last he began: “Mother, we aren't as badly off as you believe. The ship will reach us one day. If only you could trust that, and put your trust in me.... Mother, I am a poet, truly, in every part of my soul. Don't suppose these are a child's fantasies, or fantasies nourished on conceit. If you could know the thankful pride I feel in whatever is finest in me, the humble happiness with which I say this, so free of self, so distant from boasting, you would believe exactly what I want you to believe. My dearest, dearest mother! I _will_ join those who struggle for the highest things, and I give you my word that I won't betray them, that I will remain true to myself and to my gift. I will accept nothing less than the best. There can be no compromise, mother! If I test my work's weight and find the metal isn't pure, or strike it and hear a crack, a fault, back it goes into the crucible! Each thing I make must be the finest I can make! Do you understand why I must pledge myself? Gratitude for what I possess compels me to make these promises, and you must be the one to hear them. If I break them, I will have wronged you. It is you who made my soul a room with a soaring vault. Your wishes and your dreams set its growth in motion; your responsiveness and your unfulfilled hunger for beauty dedicated me to the work of my life.”

Mrs. Lyhne's tears fell without a sound. She could feel delight draining the colour from her face. She gently set both hands upon her son's head; he softly brought them down to his mouth and kissed them.

“Niels, you've given me such happiness! My whole life hasn't simply been a long, fruitless sigh, then, if I've helped you forward as I so passionately wished and imagined—heaven knows how often I imagined it! How often! And still, Niels, there's so much sorrow woven through my happiness! To have the wish dearest to me granted, the one I've cherished for all these years.... Things like that only happen when one's life is nearly over.”
“Don't say such things, you mustn't! Everything is turning out well, and you're gaining strength day by day, dear mother, aren't you?”

“Dying is so difficult,” she murmured. “Can you guess what filled my mind through those long nights without sleep, when death felt so frightfully close? What seemed most bitter was knowing how much that was magnificent and beautiful lay out in the world, and that I would have to leave it all unseen. I thought of the countless souls those things had raised up and flooded with joy and life, when for me they might never have existed. I felt my soul would take flight like a pauper on frail wings, carrying no golden recollections, no reflected brightness from the splendours of its native country, because it had spent its time beside the hearth hearing tales of the marvellous world. Niels, nobody can conceive the torment of being shut inside a dreary, darkened sickroom, trying with a fevered imagination to summon the loveliness of countries one has never visited: the white summits of the Alps above lakes of deepest blue, shining rivers flowing between vineyards, long mountain ranges where ruins show among the trees, and then immense rooms peopled with gods of marble. You never quite manage it; you abandon it and begin again, because leaving without the smallest share in it seems so cruelly hard.... Oh God, Niels, to crave it with your entire being and feel yourself being carried, slowly, towards the entrance of another world; to pause on that threshold looking back, looking so long, while something drives you through a doorway beyond which none of your desires have ever travelled.... When your turn comes to enjoy that splendour, darling, take me with you in your thoughts, into all that I will never, never be allowed to see!”
Her tears came.

Niels did what he could to soothe her. He devised ambitious journeys they would make together once her health was fully restored. He would visit a doctor in the city, he said, and surely the doctor would agree that travel was the very best course. Hadn't so-and-so gone away and come back entirely cured, simply because of the change? A change could often accomplish miracles. He laid out their itinerary down to its smallest particulars: the warm clothes he would bundle her in, the brief stages they would travel at first, the entertaining diary they would write. They would observe every tiny detail. How amusing it would be to dine on the oddest dishes in the most beautiful settings, and what dreadful crimes against grammar they would commit to begin with.

He talked like this through the whole evening and the succeeding days, without tiring of it. She joined him in the project as she might join in an agreeable daydream, though she clearly believed it could never actually happen.

Niels nevertheless followed the doctor's counsel and continued arranging everything their journey would require. She allowed him his way, even letting him choose their departure date, certain that _the thing_ would occur which must wreck all his preparations. But at last the date was only a few days away. Her youngest brother, who would run the farm while they were gone, had actually arrived. Her certainty began to waver, and now she was the one impatient to leave. Somewhere in her mind the fear still hid that, at the final instant, the obstacle would spring up and block their road.
And so they departed.

On their first day she remained fretful and anxious, with some residue of the old dread. Only after the day ended safely could she begin to believe that she truly was travelling towards the wonders she had wanted so desperately. A fever of happiness seized her then. Exuberant expectation coloured everything she said or thought, and her mind returned ceaselessly to the gifts the days ahead would bring, each in its turn.

Everything did indeed arrive, everything she had wished for. Yet it neither transported her nor stirred her with the force and warmth she had anticipated. She had pictured the sights differently, and herself differently too. In poetry and in dreams it had all lain, so to speak, across the sea. A veil of distance had mysteriously covered the restless confusion of particulars, leaving the great outlines clear and strong, while the hush of that distance supplied its enchantment. Beauty had been easy to receive then. Now she stood among these things, with every small detail asserting itself and clamouring in reality's many voices. Beauty broke apart like light passing through a prism, and she could not reunite its scattered beams; she could not set the picture back across the sea. In discouragement she had to acknowledge how poor she felt, hemmed in by riches she was unable to possess.

She wanted to press onward, always farther, hoping for somewhere she could recognize as a fragment of her imagined world. Yet every step towards that world appeared to put out the magical radiance around it. Before her disappointed gaze it spread in the ordinary illumination of the sun and moon that shone for everyone. Her search brought nothing. The year was getting late, and they hurried to Clarens, where the doctor recommended passing the winter. One last weak glimmer of hope also drew her there, that weary soul still wrapped in dreams. Was this not Rousseau's Clarens, Julie's Paradise!

They stayed there. Winter softened his manner and withheld his icy breath from her, but without effect; he had no remedy for the fever in her veins. When Spring made his victorious progress through the valley, bringing the miracle of germinating seeds and the good news of unfolding leaves, he too was forced to go past her, leaving her to fade amid all that lavish rebirth. Light, air, earth, and water sent strength pouring towards her, but it would not turn to strength inside her. It could neither intoxicate her blood with health nor make it lift its joyful voice in the mighty hymn to Spring's all-powerful rule. She could only fade. That final dream, which in her shadowed home had risen like the red promise of dawn, the dream of the far world's splendours, had brought no daylight after it. As she approached, its colours grew fainter. She knew they looked faint because the colours she had wanted were absent from life, because the beauty she craved could never ripen on earth. Yet her desire did not die. Quietly and fiercely it burned within her, fiercer for its unsatisfied thirst, a heat that consumed her.

Spring held his festival around her, heavy with the promise of beauty. The white bells of snowdrops rang it open; crocuses raised their delicately veined cups in joyful greeting. Hundreds of little streams flung themselves down the mountains into the valley, hurrying to announce Spring's arrival. Too late, all of them: as they slipped between green banks, yellow primroses and blue violets nodded to them, saying, We know it, we know it; we knew before you did! Willows opened yellow flags. Curling ferns and velvet moss draped the bare vineyard walls with green festoons, while beneath them dry nettles concealed the stones behind long edgings of brown, green, and a trace of purple. Grass laid its green cloak over the land, and lovely flowers beyond counting settled on it: hyacinths carrying star-shaped flowers and pearl-shaped flowers, crowds of daisies, gentians, anemones, dandelions, and a hundred more. Above the blossoms at ground level, a thousand brilliant islands of flowers seemed to float in the air, held aloft by the grey trunks of ancient cherry trees. Light broke in foam along their white coasts, where red and blue butterflies alighted, bearing news from the continent of flowers below.

Each new day pushed more flowers from the soil, weaving coloured designs in the gardens beside the water and spilling blossoms over the trees there: paullinias resembling enormous violets, magnolias like gigantic tulips stained purple. Flowers marched beside the pathways in ranks of white and blue, and crowded the fields in yellow hosts. But the thickest abundance filled the small protected valleys higher in the hills. There larches displayed cones like sparkling rubies against their pale needles, and narcissi opened in dazzling multitudes, sending the heavy, sleep-inducing perfume of their white revels far through the air.

Surrounded by such loveliness, she still sat with the same old hunger for beauty unanswered within her. Only occasionally could nature enchant her senses: when the sun dropped behind Savoy's soft slopes, and the mountains across the water looked like dark brown glass that admitted no light, as if their sheer faces had absorbed it all. Then evening's luminous yellow haze would hide the far-off Jura Mountains. The lake became a copper looking-glass, sending tongues of golden fire into the sunset's red radiance, until water and sky seemed to dissolve into a single shining boundlessness. At such moments, very rarely, it seemed her longing had fallen quiet and her soul had reached the country it had been seeking.

As the spring wore on, she grew steadily weaker. Before long she could no longer rise from bed. But death had ceased to frighten her: she looked forward to it impatiently. She hoped that on the other side of the grave she would meet all that magnificence face to face, that her soul would merge with the complete beauty that had called her through earthly hope and longing. The mounting pain of long, unfulfilled years had purified and transformed that longing, making it ready at last to achieve its end. She dreamed many soft, wistful dreams of remembering what the earth had offered her, returning to it in thought from immortality's country, where every earthly beauty would forever lie across the sea.

And so her life ended. Niels laid her to rest in the welcoming churchyard of Clarens, where the brown soil of the vineyards lies over people born in many countries, and where broken pillars and draped urns speak the same grief in so many different tongues.

White, they shine beneath the dark cypresses and amid the viburnum's winter flowers. Early roses scatter petals on many of them, and violets often colour the earth at their feet blue. Yet across every stone and mound the soft periwinkle trails its glossy leaves, Rousseau's beloved flower, blue with a sky-blue deeper than any sky has ever worn.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Niels Lyhne hastened back home. Alone among so many unknown faces, he could no longer endure being abroad. Yet as Copenhagen drew nearer, he asked himself more and more often what he expected to find there, and increasingly wished he had stayed away. Who was there for him in Copenhagen? Certainly not Frithjof. Erik, travelling through Italy on a scholarship, was absent too. Mrs. Boye? His connection with Mrs. Boye was a curious business. Coming directly from his mother's grave, he could not call it a profanation, precisely, or anything of that sort; yet it jarred against the pitch of his present feelings. It sounded a false note. Had he been returning to a fiancée, a youthful, blushing bride, that would have accorded with a heart occupied so long by a son's duties. He tried loftily dismissing this altered view of his attachment to Mrs. Boye as provincial and Philistine, but achieved nothing. Without his consciously choosing it, the word “Bohemian” rose to express a distaste no reasoning could remove. Accordingly, once he had secured his old lodgings on the embankment, he paid his first call to the Neergaards instead of Mrs. Boye.
He went to see her the next day, but she was out. The janitor told him she had rented a villa at Emiliekilde. Niels was surprised: he knew her father's country place stood in that same neighbourhood.
Well, in a day or two he would make the journey out.

The very next morning, however, a note arrived from Mrs. Boye, asking him to see her at her town apartment. Her pale niece had noticed him in the street. He was to arrive at a quarter to one; he _must_ be there. She would explain the reason, _unless he already knew_. Did he know? He mustn't think badly of her, or behave unreasonably.
