Remembering Fjordby, he felt a kind of immunity, like a man just through a grave sickness who knows that, having suffered his appointed torment and burnt the fever to ashes within himself, he will remain safe for a long, long while.

One summer day, after two years of Erik and Fennimore's marriage, a letter arrived from Erik, part complaint and part boast. He reproached himself for recently letting time go to waste. Something was wrong, he couldn't say what; no ideas came. His neighbours were splendid, cheerful fellows, free from fuss or convention, but absolute dromedaries where art was concerned. There wasn't a soul with whom he could talk. He had sunk into a bog of inertia and laziness and couldn't get out. Not a flicker of an idea, not a mood, not a trace of inspiration visited him. Sometimes he feared his powers were exhausted and he would never produce anything again. Yet surely this couldn't last for ever! The gift must return. He had possessed too much to finish like this. When it returned he would teach those fellows who painted perpetually, as if they had memorized the trick, what art really was. Just now, though, he was under a spell. Niels would be doing him a kindness by coming to Mariagerfjord. They would look after him as well as their circumstances permitted, and he could spend his holiday there as comfortably as elsewhere. Fennimore sent her affection and would welcome a visit.

The letter sounded so unlike Erik that Niels immediately sensed a serious trouble: otherwise he would never have complained like that. He also knew how little water fed the spring of Erik's work, a thin flow easily dried up by unfavourable conditions. He would leave immediately! Despite everything, Erik would discover a loyal friend in him. Whatever bonds the years had slackened and whatever old beliefs they had uprooted, this childhood friendship at least he would preserve. He had helped Erik once and would help him again. Friendship became a kind of fanaticism. For Erik he would surrender his own future, renown, ambitions, everything. Whatever creative restlessness and smouldering enthusiasm he possessed would belong to Erik. He would pour all his thoughts, all himself, into his friend, reserving nothing, keeping no share. For the man who had so violently torn his life apart he dreamed of greatness. For himself he imagined erasure, neglect, poverty, the forfeiture of his intellectual inheritance. In his dream the gift ceased to be a loan and became Erik's property outright, as Erik minted it into deeds and works bearing his own mark. Erik would shine in honour and glory; Niels would be merely one among the innumerable ordinary people. At last poor because he must be, rather than because he chose; a true beggar instead of a disguised prince.... There was sweetness in imagining so bitter a humiliation.

Dreams were only dreams, however. He laughed at himself, remembering how people who leave their own work undone always find unlimited time for other people’s. He also reflected that, once the two of them met face to face, Erik would naturally disown the letter and attempt to dismiss the whole complaint as nothing but a joke. He would certainly think it ridiculous if Niels arrived announcing himself ready to restore Erik’s creative gift. Despite all these doubts and reservations, Niels went. Deep down he believed he could help. However he questioned or explained away his motive, the feeling remained: their boyhood friendship had returned, with all its former warmth and simplicity, surviving both the years and everything those years had done.

The villa on Mariagerfjord belonged to an older couple whose poor health had obliged them to live in the south for an unspecified time. At first they expected to return within six months, so had left everything in place and made no arrangements for tenants. Consequently, when Erik took the house furnished, the description applied absolutely. It came with every ornament and family portrait, even an attic stuffed with decrepit furniture and old letters still inside the writing-desk drawers.

Erik discovered the villa on leaving Fjordby after his engagement. It offered everything they required, and he hoped to return to Italy within a year or two. He therefore persuaded Consul Claudi to delay buying furniture for them. They entered Marianelund much as guests enter a hotel, except for bringing rather more trunks than travellers commonly take.

Facing the fjord from under twenty feet away, the house looked unremarkable. Upstairs was a balcony, downstairs a veranda; behind it lay a new garden whose trees were no thicker than canes. But that garden opened directly into magnificent beech woodland, with heather-covered clearings and broad gullies between banks of white clay. This compensated for much that the place lacked.

Here was Fennimore's new home. For a time happiness lit it as brilliantly as happiness can, since both were young, healthy, vigorous, and in love, with no anxiety over sustenance for either body or spirit.

Yet the ground beneath every palace of happiness reaching towards heaven contains some sand. The grains gather and slip away, perhaps slowly, perhaps unnoticed, but they keep slipping, one by one.... And love? Love is no solid rock either, much as we want to believe otherwise.
She gave him her entire soul, loving with the burning, shaking passion that fear produces. To her he was far more, far closer, than a god: he was an idol, adored beyond reason and without restraint.

He loved as fiercely as she did, but without that fine masculine gentleness which preserves a beloved woman's dignity and defends her against herself. Dimly he recognized it as an obligation, sometimes hearing its faint call, but refusing to attend. Her unseeing devotion was too seductive. Her beauty, with a slave woman's provocative abundance and submissive allure, roused a desire in him that acknowledged neither limit nor mercy.
Doesn't the ancient story of Amor tell, somewhere, how he covers Psyche's eyes with his hand before they fly in ecstasy into the radiant night?

Unhappy Fennimore! Had the fire in her heart threatened to consume her, the man meant to protect her would have stirred it higher. He resembled the drunken emperor brandishing a torch, crying out delightedly as his imperial capital burned, growing intoxicated with the leaping blaze, until its ashes brought him to his senses.

Unhappy Fennimore! She did not realize a hymn of delight can be repeated until words and tune disappear, leaving only commonplace babble. She did not realize that today's uplifting intoxication borrows its strength from tomorrow's wings. When sobriety eventually arrived, heavy and grey, she discovered in terror that their loving had brought them down to a sweet disdain for one another and themselves. Day by day its sweetness diminished, until the disdain was nothing but bitterness. They retreated from each other as far as possible. He dreamed of his forsaken ideal, her lofty chill and proud grace; she looked with hopeless longing towards the vague, peaceful shores of her girlhood, now unimaginably remote. Each day made endurance harder. Shame raced burning through her, while suffocating self-disgust rendered everything miserable and without hope. An unused little room held only the trunks she had brought from home. Often she sat there for hours, until the sinking sun filled it with reddish light. She tormented herself with thoughts sharper than thorns and lashed herself with words crueler than whips. At last misery left her dazed, and she tried to numb the hurt by flinging herself onto the floor like something full of rot and sediment, her own dead carcass, too filthy to house a soul. Her husband's mistress! The thought never left her. With it she cast herself in the dirt and stamped upon herself; with it she shut out every prospect of renewal and petrified every joyful recollection.

By degrees a harsh, brutal apathy possessed her. She stopped despairing, as she had long ago stopped hoping. Her heaven had collapsed, and she made no attempt to rebuild its vault even in imagination. Earth was enough for one made of earth, so wholly earthy. She felt no hatred for Erik and did not withdraw from him. Instead she submitted to his kisses, too contemptuous of herself to refuse. Besides, wasn't she his wife, his woman?

Erik also found the awakening bitter, though a man's unromantic common sense had warned him that it must arrive eventually. When it did, when love stopped compensating for every sorrow and the shining golden veil in which it had appeared before him blew away, his spirits sank and all his powers grew sluggish. It frightened and angered him. He rushed to work, desperate to prove that happiness was the only thing he had lost. But art gave no reassuring reply. He seized on several unfortunate notions which he could neither develop nor decide to drop. They would not become anything, yet kept nagging at him, blocking other ideas from emerging or claiming his energies. Discouraged and dissatisfied, he settled into sulky idleness. Work was being so damned obstinate; plainly he must wait for inspiration to return. Days passed, however, and his gift stayed sterile. Nothing beside the quiet fjord could fertilize it. Nor were there fellow painters whose successes might incite him to rivalry, whether in imitation or in opposition.

Doing nothing became intolerable. A violent hunger to feel himself alive, in any fashion whatever, took hold. With no other prospect, he sought the company of local men, old and young, who relieved rural dullness with whatever indulgences their restricted imaginations could invent and their rather narrow tastes enjoy. Drinking and cards always formed the core; the outer covering might be called a hunt or a market visit. Little changed when they transferred the proceedings to a nearby town and spent an afternoon on actual or supposed dealings with shopkeepers. The transaction invariably concluded that night at the inn, where a discerning landlord directed customers of the proper kind to Number Caveat. If travelling actors happened to be visiting, the tradesmen were dropped. Actors made better company, did not avoid a bottle, and were generally willing to attempt the miraculous, though never entirely effective, remedy of using gin to sober themselves after champagne had made them drunk.

A sixty-year-old squire devoted to hunting led the group. Its regular members were chiefly neighbouring minor landowners and country gentlemen. It also included a large young dandy who distilled brandy, and a tutor with a white neckcloth who had taught nobody for twenty years or longer. He roamed from one house to another with a sealskin bag and an old grey mare, supposedly purchased from a horse butcher. A quiet drinker, he played the flute brilliantly and was reputed to know Arabic. The squire's “staff” also contained a solicitor with an unfailing stock of fresh anecdotes, and a doctor whose entire repertoire was a single story about the siege of Lübeck in the year 6.

They lived widely apart and almost never assembled in full. But let anyone absent himself too long, and the squire summoned the loyal members to inspect the deserter's oxen. Every member of the company understood perfectly what that meant: they were to lodge with the unfortunate fellow for two or three days, overturning his household with liquor, gambling, and whatever countryside entertainments the season supplied. On one such disciplinary expedition snow trapped the entire company. Coffee, sugar, and rum ran out, reducing them to a substitute coffee punch made with chicory, sweetened by syrup, and fortified with brandy.

These were rough drinking companions Erik had found. Perhaps their immense animal energy could scarcely discover an adequate release in more refined pleasures; certainly their constant good spirits and broad, bear-like merriment softened much of the coarseness. For a talent like Brouwer's or Ostade's, this select fellowship of revellers would have been a mine of gold. For his own art, Erik gained nothing except a great deal of enjoyment—too much, indeed. Before long the uproar became essential to him and consumed almost every hour. Occasionally he reproached himself and swore to stop wasting his days. Yet whenever he tried to work, emptiness and creative helplessness overtook him again and sent him back to his former habits.

He wrote to Niels on a day when the lasting barrenness made him suspect some wasting sickness had attacked his gift. The moment the letter left, he regretted sending it and hoped Niels would hear the complaint with one ear and promptly let it escape through the other.

But Niels arrived, friendship's very knight-errant, to receive that blend of pity and rebuff which has greeted such knights in every age from the people for whose benefit they dragged Rosinante from her comfortable stall. Niels had tact, though, and waited patiently. Erik soon softened and their former intimacy returned. His need to empty himself in lamentation and confession had become almost bodily in its urgency.

One night, after the usual bedtime, Fennimore went upstairs and the two remained in the dark sitting-room with cognac and water. Their cigar tips alone marked their positions. Occasionally Niels leaned well back, and his raised profile showed black against the dim window. They had drunk freely, particularly Erik, while recalling their boyhood at Lönborggaard. Fennimore's withdrawal left a pause neither wished to interrupt. Thoughts stole over them in an agreeable languor as they listened sleepily to the humming of their own blood, heated by the cognac.

At last Erik spoke. “What idiots we were at twenty. Heaven knows what on earth we imagined, or how we persuaded ourselves such things existed here. We used reality's names for them, but meant something immeasurably above this dull adequacy we've actually received. There isn't much in life, when you look at it. Is there?”

“I'm not sure. I accept what it offers. Generally we don't do very much living; most of the time we simply keep existing. If only life arrived as one enormous, tempting cake you could bite straight into ... but these tiny portions! No, there's not much pleasure in that.”

“Tell me something, Niels. You're the only person I can discuss such nonsense with; I can't explain why, you're such an odd creature. Tell me—is there any drink left in your glass? Good! Have you ever considered death?”
“Have I? Certainly. And you?”

“I don't mean when somebody's ill or at a burial. Sometimes I'm sitting perfectly comfortably and it comes upon me like—like sheer despair. Sitting here brooding, doing nothing and _unable_ to do anything, I can actually feel the time escaping. Hours, weeks, months fly past empty, and I can't pin them down with work. I don't know whether this makes sense to you, but I want to seize time by achieving something. The time spent on a painting belongs to me always. It has passed, but hasn't been wasted. Thinking of the days going by without pause makes me sick. And I _have_ nothing—or can't reach what I have. It's agony! Sometimes fury drives me to my feet, and I pace about singing some stupid song so I won't burst into tears. When I stop, the thought almost maddens me: meanwhile more time has gone, and while I'm thinking it still goes, goes, goes. No condition is more wretched than an artist's. I'm healthy and strong; my eyes can see, my blood is hot and red, my heart works, my mind isn't damaged, and I _want_ to work, yet I can't. I struggle and feel about for something that slips away, something I couldn't catch even if I laboured until I sweated blood. What can anyone do to summon inspiration, to obtain an idea? Whether I concentrate or go out pretending to seek nothing makes no difference. Nothing ever comes, only the sense of Time standing waist-deep in eternity and pulling in the hours. They race past, twelve white ones and twelve black ones, without halting, without halting. What am I to do? What do other people do when this happens? I can't be the first. Can you offer nothing?”
“Go travelling.”
“No, not that, anything else. Why suggest that? You don't think it's all over for me?”
“Over for you! Certainly not. I meant that fresh impressions—”

“Fresh impressions! Precisely. Haven't you heard of people gifted in their earliest youth, when everything was new and they were filled with hopes and intentions, whose gift vanished once youth ended and never returned?”
For a long while neither spoke.

“_Those_ people travelled, Niels, hunting fresh impressions. They couldn't let go of the notion. They tried the south and the Orient, all useless; everything slipped away from them as from a mirror. In Rome I've seen their graves, two of them, though there are many, many more. One lost his mind.”
“I've never come across that happening to painters.”

“It happens. What explains it, do you suppose? Some unseen nerve giving way? Or perhaps we've failed something inside ourselves, committed a sin against it—who knows? The soul is terribly delicate, and nobody knows how far through a person it reaches. We ought to treat ourselves kindly, Niels!” His voice softened and fell. “I've often wanted to travel because of this emptiness. You can't imagine how desperately I've wanted it. But I simply dare not. Suppose it did no good, and I turned out to belong among those people? What then! Imagine knowing beyond doubt that I was finished, possessed nothing, could accomplish nothing—imagine it, nothing! A worthless wretch, a damned crippled dog, a pitiful eunuch! What would happen to me, do you think? It isn't out of the question, after all. My first youth has ended. As for illusions and suchlike, I can promise you there aren't many left. We use them up frightfully fast, and I never even wanted to shed mine. I wasn't like you and the others gathered at Mrs. Boye's: always busy pulling one another's beautiful feathers out, crowing louder the barer you became. But does it matter? Sooner or later every one of us begins to moult.”
Silence returned. Cognac weighted the air, and acrid cigar fumes filled it. They sighed miserably, oppressed equally by the stuffy room and the sadness of their own hearts.

Niels had come two hundred miles to help, and now sat ashamed of the impulse while the colder part of himself watched. What could he actually accomplish? Speak to Erik in glowing pictures, perhaps, in plentiful purple and ultramarine language soaked with light and deep in shadow! He had entertained something of that dream before setting out. How completely ridiculous! Bringing help! At most you might chase the closed-handed goddess from an artist's threshold. You could no more help him create than, if paralysis struck, you could enable him to lift his own little finger. No amount of overflowing affection, understanding, devotion, or other generous feeling could do it.... You ought to attend to your own concerns. That was wholesome and useful. Naturally it was easier to let your heart charge about in a grand display of generosity. Its unfortunate defect was being hopelessly impractical and entirely ineffectual. Looking after your own business and doing it properly might not win you heaven, but at least it left you able to meet the eyes of God and man alike.

Niels had ample occasion to brood on a good heart's helplessness. His only achievement was keeping Erik at home a little more often for a month or so. Still, he had no desire to go back to Copenhagen in the heat. Unwilling to remain a guest without limit, he rented a room across the fjord with a family slightly above the peasant class, close enough to reach Marianelund in a quarter-hour's rowing. Having grown accustomed to the district, he preferred it as much as any other place. He was susceptible to the hold surroundings can acquire over certain people. Besides, his friend and his cousin Fennimore were here: reason enough, particularly when there was nobody anywhere else waiting for him.

On the journey from Copenhagen he had carefully planned his manner towards Fennimore. He would make it plain that he had forgotten so thoroughly he no longer even remembered anything needing to be forgotten. Above all there must be no chilliness: amiable detachment, surface warmth, courteous concern. That was the right approach.
Every bit of that preparation proved useless.

The Fennimore before him was not the woman he had left. Her beauty remained: the same luxuriant figure, the same languid, unhurried movements that had once enchanted him. But her mouth wore the bleak vacancy of someone who has done too much thinking; in her gentle eyes was a pitiable, tormented cruelty. He could make nothing of it. One thing, however, was obvious: remembering him had occupied very little of her attention, and any recollections he might revive left her untouched. She looked like someone who had chosen her course and made the worst possible use of it.
Slowly he began deciphering the signs and connecting them. Then, one day on a walk beside the water, understanding began to come.

Erik was tidying the studio. As Niels and Fennimore walked along the shore, the maid appeared carrying an apronful of rubbish and emptied it onto the beach: worn brushes, pieces of plaster casts, snapped palette knives, shards of oil bottles, and squeezed-out paint tubes. Niels nudged the heap with his shoe while Fennimore watched, sharing that aimless curiosity old discarded things so often provoke. Suddenly he jerked his foot away as if burnt. He immediately recovered himself and kicked at the rubbish again.
“Please, let me look,” Fennimore said, laying a hand on his arm to stop him. Niels then stooped down and extracted a plaster hand holding an egg.
“Surely this got thrown away by mistake,” he said.

Taking it, she answered evenly, “No, look, it's damaged. The first finger is missing.” She pointed to the break. Then she noticed that the egg had been sliced open and its inside painted with a chrome-yellow yolk. She flushed, bent down, and struck the hand against a stone, slowly and deliberately, until nothing remained but small fragments.
To break the silence, Niels asked, “Do you recall when that cast was made?”
“I recall having green soap spread over my hand to keep the plaster from sticking. Were you remembering that?”

“I meant when Erik handed it round during tea. Do you remember exactly what happened when your old aunt received it? Tears came into her eyes, and she hugged you so compassionately and kissed your forehead, as though somebody had hurt you.”
“Yes, people have such tender feelings.”
“We all laughed at her, certainly. Yet for all its absurdity there was something finely sensitive in what she did.”
“Yes, the world contains plenty of finely sensitive absurdity.”
“I suspect you're looking for an argument with me today.”

“I'm not. There is something I do want to tell you, though. You won't resent my being a little direct? Well, imagine a husband tells a rather indecent story in front of his wife, or behaves in some other way that strikes you as inconsiderate towards her. Isn't it unnecessary for you to register disapproval by becoming conspicuously delicate and extravagantly chivalrous? Surely one may assume he understands his own wife best, and knows she won't be hurt or offended. Otherwise he wouldn't behave so. Isn't that fair?”
“As a general principle, no, it isn't. In this particular instance, though, and taking your word for it, I'm willing to agree.”

“Good. Believe me, women aren't the creatures of pure air so many well-meaning young men imagine. They're no more sensitive than men, really, and not so different in other respects. You can trust me: dirty clay went into the making of both.”
“My dear Fennimore! Thank heaven you don't understand your own words. You're wronging women, and wronging yourself. _I_ have faith in women's purity.”
“Women's purity! What exactly is this purity of women?”
“What I mean is—well—”

“I'll tell you what you mean: nothing. That's another of those delicate absurdities. A woman cannot be pure, and isn't intended to be. How could she be? Nature forbids it! Do you imagine God created her for purity? Tell me! No, a thousand times no, ten thousand. Why persist in this madness! Why toss us among the stars with one hand if the other must drag us back! Can't we stay on the ground alongside you, simply people with other people, and nothing beyond that? How can our feet find firm ground in life's prose when your poetic marsh-lights dazzle us? Leave us in peace! In God's name, leave us in peace!”
She dropped into a seat and began crying.

Niels saw a great deal now. Fennimore would have been distressed to know quite how much. Wasn't this partly the familiar tale of love's feast that won't become everyday bread, but remains a feast while growing daily flatter, more flavourless, less sustaining? Neither partner can work the miracle. They sit in their festive finery, remembering to smile and speak in celebratory tones, while underneath hunger and thirst torment them, their eyes avoid each other, and hatred takes root. Wasn't that the opening chapter? And didn't the next contain the equally miserable story of a woman unable to regain herself after discovering the half-divine being she so joyfully married was merely human? First despair, useless despair, followed by merciful numbness: surely that explained it. Niels believed he understood all of her now, the hardness, the desolate submissiveness, the coarseness that was the cup's most bitter drop. Slowly he understood as well why his consideration and respectful homage must burden and annoy her. A woman flung from her dreams' purple couch onto the paving stones soon resents someone carpeting the hardness she longs to feel. In the first anguish she will not settle for walking the road on her feet. She insists on crawling upon her knees, selecting its roughest, steepest stretch. She rejects any offered hand and refuses to raise her head. Let its own weight drag it down, until her face touches the earth and her tongue can taste the dust!
His whole heart ached for her; nevertheless he respected her wish to be left alone.

Watching without helping was difficult: sitting apart dreaming up foolish happiness for her, or waiting with a doctor's cold calculation of how long the suffering must continue. In that bleak wisdom he told himself relief could come only after her old faith in life's shining treasures had bled away. A slower current must replace it in her veins, dulling her enough to forget, blunting her enough to submit, until finally she was coarse enough to take pleasure in the thick air of a happiness many heavens below the one she had humbly prayed and meekly hoped to reach on wings. Thinking of it filled him with disgust at the world. This woman, before whom he had once knelt in reverence, had been brought to slavery; she stood shivering outside the gate while he rode by on his fine horse with life's great coins rattling in his pockets.

Late in August, one Sunday afternoon, Niels rowed over the fjord. Fennimore was alone. He discovered her stretched on the corner room's sofa in great distress, breathing with the soft, steady moan that seems to ease pain. She complained of a terrible headache. There was nobody to look after her: she had allowed the maid to visit home in Hadssund, and soon afterward somebody had arrived and taken Erik away. Where they could have gone in such rain she couldn't imagine. For two hours she had lain trying to sleep, but the pain prevented it. Nothing like this had happened before, and it began so abruptly; at dinner she had been perfectly well. First her temples hurt, then the pain seemed to bore farther and farther inward. Now it was behind her eyes. She only hoped it wasn't dangerous. Unaccustomed to illness, she was frightened and thoroughly miserable.

Niels offered what reassurance he could. He told her to keep still, shut her eyes, and stop talking. Finding a thick shawl, he tucked it around her feet. He brought vinegar from the sideboard, prepared a cool compress, and placed it across her forehead. Then he quietly took a chair beside the window and watched the rainfall.

At intervals he tiptoed back to replace the cloth, saying nothing, only nodding as her grateful eyes looked up between his hands. Once or twice she tried to speak; he silenced her with a glance and a shake of his head, then went back to the window.
Eventually sleep took her.

An hour went by, then another, and her sleep continued. Quarter followed quarter without a break. The sad daylight weakened, while shadows enlarged about the room as though sprouting out of walls and furniture. Beyond the windows the rain fell at an unchanging pace, its quiet, continuous pattering smothering every other noise.
Still her sleep went on.

Vinegar vapour mingled with the heliotrope's vanilla perfume, filling the room with a sharp, wine-like smell. Their breathing warmed the air, coating the grey panes with moisture; as evening grew colder, the mist on the windows thickened.

By now Niels had wandered deep into recollection and reverie, though some part of him remained beside the sleeping woman, attending to her rest. As darkness gathered, his imagination tired of sustaining dreams that flared and subsided, as ground exhausts itself growing the same crop repeatedly. The visions weakened, grew barren and stiff, and lost the luxuriant particulars that had wound about them like long tendrils. His thoughts left the distance and returned home. What stillness surrounded them! He and she seemed alone on a silent island above the unvarying sea of sound made by the rain's gentle tapping. Their souls were quiet, safe, at rest; the future itself seemed asleep in a cradle of peace.

If only the future need never wake, and everything could stay this way: no happiness beyond peace, but no misery either, no gnawing disquiet! If only the present could fold around itself like a closing bud, with no spring to follow it!

Fennimore called to him. She had been awake awhile, too delighted by the absence of pain to consider speaking. Now she proposed getting up and lighting the lamp. Niels, continuing in his role as doctor, insisted she remain lying down. Rising wasn't good for her yet. He had matches and would have no trouble locating the lamp.

He lit it and set it on the plant stand in a corner. Its milky globe glowed gently behind a veil of the acacia's fine, sleeping leaves. There was just enough illumination for them to make out one another's faces.
Seated opposite her, he talked with her about the weather: how fortunate Erik had remembered his raincoat, how soaked poor Trine would be. After these remarks their conversation ran out.

Fennimore's mind had not entirely woken. In her weakened state, lying silently with her thoughts was pleasant. Niels felt little wish to speak either; the afternoon's long hush still held him under its spell.
Finally Fennimore asked, “Does this house please you?”
“Yes, on the whole it does.”
“Does it? Can you recall our furniture at home?”
“In Fjordby? Certainly, I remember it very clearly.”

“You can't imagine my affection for it, how I sometimes miss it. None of these things are ours; we rent them. They carry no memories, and we'll leave them behind when we leave the house. Perhaps it sounds odd, but among these unfamiliar pieces I often feel quite lonely. They stand about looking stupid and indifferent, accepting whatever I am without the least concern for me. Knowing they won't accompany me anywhere, that they'll simply remain for the next tenants, I can't grow attached to them or care about them as I would if they were always to share my home. Then whatever happiness or sorrow came would happen among them. Do you find that childish? It may be. Still, I can't change the way I feel about it.”

“I can't explain it, but I've felt something similar. After I was left alone abroad my watch stopped working. When the watchmaker returned it, ticking again as usual, I felt exactly what you're describing. It was a welcome sensation, peculiar, but with something sincerely good in it.”
“Yes, exactly! In your place, I think I would have kissed the watch.”
“Would you really?”
Suddenly she said, “You know, you've told me nothing about Erik's childhood. What sort of boy was he?”
“Everything admirable and good, Fennimore. Brave, magnificent: the boy other boys dream of being. Perhaps not the model child a teacher or mother imagines, but the other kind, and so much better.”
“And how were things between you? Did you love each other very much?”

“I adored him, and he let me: that more or less describes it. We were unlike one another. I always meant to become a celebrated poet. One day I asked what he wanted to be; can you guess his answer? An Indian, a real red Indian, war paint and everything! I remember being utterly bewildered. How could anyone wish to be a savage? To my civilized mind it was impossible to understand!”
“Then wasn't becoming an artist rather strange for him?” Fennimore asked. Something chilly and antagonistic entered her voice with the question.

Niels registered it with a small shock. “Not in the least,” he said. “People rarely become artists with every part of their character. Strong, overflowing natures such as Erik's often feel an indescribable hunger for delicacy and refinement: an exquisite virginal coolness, a noble sweetness. I can hardly find the words. Outside they may look vigorous and hearty, even rough. Nobody guesses the curious romantic and sentimental mysteries they keep inside. They're shy, you see, shy in their spirits; no pale young girl guards her soul more bashfully than these great heavy-footed men. Can't you see, Fennimore, how a secret that cannot be uttered plainly in the air of ordinary life might turn somebody towards art? They cannot say it directly, simply cannot. We must trust that it exists and quietly lives within them, like a bulb underground. Every so often they send fine-coloured, fragrant flowers up into daylight. Do you see? Ask nothing for yourself from this power to blossom. Trust it, be glad to sustain it and to know it's there. Forgive me, Fennimore, but I feel you and Erik aren't treating each other kindly. Couldn't that change? Don't ask who is right, or how serious the offence, and don't give him merely what he deserves. How would the best of us survive being given only our deserts! Think of him instead as he was when you loved him most deeply. He deserves that, believe me. You mustn't weigh and reckon. I know love has moments of such radiant, solemn rapture that we'd willingly give our lives for the loved one, if required. Isn't that so? Remember those moments now, Fennimore, for yourself and for him.”
He fell quiet.
She remained silent too, lying perfectly motionless, flower-pale, with a sad smile upon her mouth.
Then she raised herself partway and offered Niels her hand. “Will you be a friend to me?” she asked.
Taking it, he said, “You already have my friendship, Fennimore.”
“Can I trust that, Niels?”
“Always,” he answered, respectfully bringing her hand up to kiss it.
As he stood, Fennimore thought she had never before seen him hold himself so upright.
Soon afterward Trine appeared to say she was back. Tea followed, and eventually Niels rowed home again through the dismal rain.

Erik returned near morning. In dawn's cold, honest light Fennimore watched him getting ready for bed: sodden with drink, unsteady and heavy, his eyes glazed by cards and his sleepless face a dirty pallor. Every beautiful thing Niels had said seemed unreal to her then. The shining pledges she had made inwardly weakened and lost colour before the advancing daylight. Misty dreams, vapours of imagination, a whole fairy host of falsehoods!

Why struggle against the weight pulling them both under? Pretence could not lessen it, and their lives would never float freely as before. Frost had passed over them. The mass of vines, climbing tendrils, clustered roses, and flowers lovelier than roses that once wound about them had dropped every leaf and every bloom. Only tough, bare stems remained, tying them together with bonds that could not break. What good was it to warm old emotions artificially with memories, to lift her idol back onto its plinth, to summon admiration into her gaze, worship onto her tongue, and happy colour into her face! What good, if he refused to serve as the idol's priest and assist in that pious deception? He! He no longer even recalled her love. None of her words lingered in his hearing; not one of their shared days lay treasured inside him.

The passionate love between them was cold and dead. Its scent, its magic, its trembling music had all drifted away. Habit seated them together, his arm about her, her head upon his shoulder, sunk in dreary silence and forgetting one another. She remembered the splendid hero he had never actually been; he recast her in imagination as the ideal now shining perpetually far above her. That was their married life. Days followed days and altered nothing. Each day they surveyed the wasteland before them, repeating to themselves that it was a wasteland, without flowers, without hope of flowers, of springs, of green palm trees.

Through the autumn Erik's drinking expeditions grew more frequent. As he told Niels, why sit waiting at home for ideas that never arrived until his thoughts petrified inside his skull? Besides, Niels's companionship offered little comfort. He needed people of substance, vigorous flesh-and-blood creatures, not a fanciful bundle of sensitive nerves. Consequently Niels, who crossed to Marianelund daily, spent a great deal of time alone with Fennimore.

Their promise of friendship and their conversation that Sunday removed the awkwardness between them. Both lonely, they grew close in an affectionate, gentle companionship that soon gripped them strongly. It occupied their minds whether they were together or separated. Everything they thought returned to their bond, as birds building a nest examine whatever they find or pass with a single pleasant purpose: to make their shared shelter comfortable and snug for one another and themselves.

When Erik was out, Niels and Fennimore almost always went walking for hours in the woodland beyond the garden, even through wind and rain. They had come to love the forest, and loved it more as they watched its summer life disappear. A thousand changes demanded attention. Leaves first became yellow, red, and brown, then fell: in windy weather they wheeled in yellow flocks, in stillness they rustled softly downward one by one, past rigid limbs and between yielding brown twigs. As trees and shrubs lost their foliage, nest after nest exposed summer's hidden secrets. Branches and ground offered treasures: delicate seeds, vivid berries, brown nuts, polished acorns with their elegant cups, coral tassels hanging from barberry, glossy black buckthorn fruit, scarlet rose-hip urns. Prickly beech nuts dotted the naked beeches; the rowan bowed beneath red bunches whose sharp scent recalled cider. Along the paths late blackberries lay brown and black among damp leaves. Red whortleberries appeared in the heather, and wild raspberry bushes bore their muted crimson fruit a second time. Fading ferns assumed every colour. The moss was a discovery in itself: not just the thick, lush growth on slopes and in hollows, but the pale, fine patches on trunks. These resembled imagined elfin cornfields, sending up the slenderest stems, each tipped with a dark brown bud like an ear of grain.

They explored the wood from edge to edge, intent on discovering every wonder and treasure. Like children, they apportioned it: everything to one side of the road belonged to Fennimore, everything opposite to Niels. They compared their territories and argued over which possessed greater splendours. Each hollow and mound, track and stile, ditch and pond acquired a name; an especially magnificent tree received one too. Thus they made the place entirely theirs, inventing a little country unknown to anybody else, where no other person felt at home. Yet they shared no secret that everyone in the world might not safely have overheard.
Not yet, at any rate.

Love both existed in their hearts and did not exist, as crystals exist within a saturated liquid yet remain absent until a splinter, the tiniest fragment of suitable matter, enters it. Then, as though enchanted, the sleeping atoms awaken, fly towards one another, and fasten together by inscrutable laws. In an instant there are crystals, crystals everywhere.
A similarly tiny event revealed their love to them.

There is scarcely a story to relate. On an ordinary day they were alone in the sitting-room, as they had been a hundred times. They talked of unimportant matters, and outwardly what occurred was as everyday as anything could be. Niels was standing at the window, looking outside. Fennimore joined him and looked outside too. Nothing more. Yet it sufficed. In a lightning flash, awareness changed Niels Lyhne's past, present, and future: he loved this woman beside him. He did not love her as some bright, sweet, beautiful happiness that would bear him into rapture. That was not what his love meant. He loved her as something as indispensable as breathing. He reached for her like a drowning man reaching for a hold and pressed her hand against his heart.

She understood. An answer and an admission escaped her, almost a scream, her voice full of anguish and fright: “Oh, _yes_, Niels!” At the same instant she tore her hand free. For a moment she remained standing, white and recoiling, then dropped one knee onto a padded chair, buried her face in the back's rough velvet, and sobbed audibly.

For several seconds Niels seemed blinded, feeling about among the bulb glasses for something to steady him. Only a few seconds passed before he went to her chair. He bent above her without touching her, one hand braced on the chair's back.
“Don't torment yourself so, Fennimore! Look at me; let's speak about it. Will you try? Don't be frightened! We must carry this together, my love! Come, try to do that!”
She lifted her face a little towards him. “Oh God, what can we do! Niels, how dreadful this is! Why must it happen to me? It could all have been so beautiful, so happy!” Then the sobs returned.
“Ought I to have kept silent?” he groaned. “My poor Fennimore, would you prefer never to have found out?”
Again she lifted her head and grasped his hand. “I wish I knew and were dead. To lie in my grave and know it—that would be good, so peaceful, so wonderfully good!”
“How bitter, Fennimore, for both of us, that sorrow and weeping should be our love's very first gift. Don't you feel that?”

“Don't judge me harshly, Niels. I can't stop it. You can't see it from my side. The strength ought to come from me, because I'm the one already bound. I wish I could seize this love, thrust it back into the deepest hidden part of my soul, and lock it away, refusing to hear its cries and pleadings. Then I could send you far, far off. But I can't. I've endured so much, I can't endure that as well, Niels, I can't. Without you I can't live. Can I? Do you believe I could?”
She got up and threw herself against his chest.

“I'm here, and I refuse to release you. I won't send you off and remain alone in that old darkness. It's a pit without a bottom, full of misery and disgust. I won't cast myself back into it. I'd sooner leap into the fjord, Niels. This new life may bring fresh torments, but at least they'll be fresh. They won't carry the old dull ache, won't strike so deep as the old ones that understand my heart with such cruelty. Am I speaking wildly? Yes, naturally. But how good it is to speak to you without holding back, without watching lest I say something forbidden. Your claim comes before every other now! I wish you could possess me completely, make me entirely yours and nobody else's. If only you could lift me out of every tie that hems me in!”
“We have to break those ties, Fennimore. I'll make the best arrangements I can. Have no fear! Before anyone guesses, we'll be far from here.”

“No, we can't flee, not that. Anything else, anything rather than my parents hearing that their daughter has run away. That's impossible! I'll never consent. As God lives in heaven, Niels, I will never do that.”

“But you must, darling, you must. Don't you see the ugliness and meanness that will gather around us if we remain? The deceit and lies will bind us and pull us under. I won't let all that smear you. I won't allow it to rust away our love from within.”
She would not yield an inch.

Sadly he said, “You don't understand the sentence you're passing on us. Better to trample things beneath iron feet now than try to spare them. Believe me, Fennimore, our love must come before everything, must be our one concern, the thing we save even if saving it means wounding where we'd rather heal and causing sorrow where we'd gladly banish its smallest shadow. Unless we do that, the yoke we're accepting will grow heavier until it drives us to our knees, pitilessly, inevitably. Fighting on your knees—you can't imagine how hard that is! Still, shall we fight, little one, together against everything?”

During the first few days Niels kept urging her to leave with him. Then he began imagining Erik returning to discover his wife and friend had fled together, and the hurt it would cause. Gradually the whole scheme acquired an excessively tragic, impossible air. He trained himself not to consider it, just as he avoided many other things he would have preferred otherwise, and gave himself entirely to the circumstances they actually had. He made no deliberate effort to transform them by dreaming, or decorate their defects with imaginary garlands. Yet how sweet it was, for once, to love within real life. Now he understood that none of his supposed earlier loves had been true love: not the solitary young man's swollen longing, not the dreamer's ardent hunger, not even the child's uneasy foreknowledge. They had been currents in love's ocean, isolated reflections of its whole light, broken pieces of love as meteors travelling through space are broken pieces of a planet. Love was precisely that: a complete world, rounded, immense, ordered. It was no jumble of disordered feelings and moods tumbling over each other! Like nature, it altered perpetually and renewed itself. No emotion faded, no feeling died, without bringing alive the seed it held of something more perfect still. Loving with his whole being, quietly and healthily, drawing full, deep breaths: how good that was. Days dropped straight out of heaven, fresh and shining as newly minted coins. They no longer succeeded each other automatically, like familiar pictures passing in a peep-show. Every day revealed something. Each made him feel stronger, larger, more generous. Never had his feelings possessed such fullness or force. Sometimes he seemed a titan to himself, greater than human, so inexhaustible was the spring within him, so vast-winged the tenderness filling his heart, so marvellous his range of vision, so boundless the kindness of his judgments.
Happiness began like this, and for a long time happiness lasted.

The routine deceit, the lies, the dishonourable atmosphere they inhabited had not yet mastered them. It could not reach the ecstatic heights to which Niels had raised their attachment and themselves with it. He was not merely a man who had seduced his friend's wife. Or rather, as he defiantly argued inwardly, he was that man, but he was also the rescuer of an innocent woman whom life had hurt, stoned, and soiled, a woman who had lain down prepared for her soul to die. He had restored her trust in life and belief in goodness, lifted her spirit to nobility, given her joy. Which was preferable, then: her earlier blameless unhappiness or what he had brought her? He wasn't asking a question. His choice was made.

Truthfully, he did not wholly believe this. Human beings often construct theories they refuse to inhabit. Thought can race ahead where conscience hesitates to follow. Yet the notion genuinely existed in his mind. It drew off some of the corrosive poison contained in their life of cunning, falsehood, and double-dealing.

Before long the damage began to show nonetheless. The poison touched too many delicate nerve fibres not to hurt them. Matters accelerated shortly after New Year, when Erik announced he had found an idea. Something in a green tunic, striking a menacing pose, he explained to Niels. Did Niels recall the green in Salvator Rosa's Jonah? Something of that kind.

Erik's labour consisted mostly of reclining on the studio couch, smoking shag tobacco, and reading Marryat. Still, it kept him indoors for the moment. That forced the lovers to greater vigilance and required further inventions and lies.

Fennimore's cleverness at these inventions cast the first shadow over their heaven. Initially it was almost invisible: a doubt as light as floating thistledown passed through Niels, suggesting that his love might be finer than the woman he loved. It had not become a definite thought, only a dim intimation pointing that way, a slight inward yielding, an inclination towards it.

But it returned and others followed. At first indistinct and cloudy, these thoughts sharpened each time they came. The speed with which they eroded, degraded, and stripped away enchantment was astonishing. Love did not diminish; indeed it burned more fiercely as it descended. Yet hands meeting secretly under tablecloths, kisses stolen in corridors or behind doors, prolonged glances exchanged before the man they betrayed—all these robbed it of elevation. Happiness no longer hovered steadily above them. They had to steal her smiles and brightness wherever possible. Eventually their tricks and stratagems ceased to be unfortunate necessities and became entertaining successes. Deception turned into their native air, making them small and despicable. Other shameful secrets, previously grieved over separately while each pretended the other knew nothing, now had to be shared. Erik had no reserve: in front of Niels he would fondle his wife, kiss her, draw her onto his knees and hold her. Conscious guilt made Fennimore fearful and hesitant; she lacked both the courage and self-respect to reject those caresses.
Thus the noble fortress of their love sank, and kept sinking: that fortress from whose towers they had surveyed the world so proudly, and within whose walls they had felt so strong and fine.
Even among its ruins, though, happiness remained.

Their woodland walks now generally took place in dismal weather, with fog suspended under black branches and gathering between dripping trunks. Nobody then could witness their embraces and kisses, here and there, or hear their careless talk breaking into bursts of licentious laughter.

The sadness of eternity that had once ennobled their love disappeared. Now they exchanged only jokes and smiles. Greedily, feverishly, they grabbed at passing instants of pleasure, as though love must hurry, as though no whole lifetime lay ahead.

Nothing altered when Erik eventually abandoned his idea and resumed drinking with such zeal that he seldom stayed home two full days together. They remained where they had fallen. Very occasionally, alone, they might look back regretfully towards their former heights. Or perhaps they simply wondered how exhausting life there must have been and felt more comfortably lodged below. There was no change, certainly no return to those earlier days. They did, however, become more conscious of the slack, sordid character of remaining as they were instead of escaping together. Shared guilt tied them into a closer, lower bond. Neither of them actually wanted to make any alteration in the existing arrangement, and neither pretended otherwise to the other. Between them had grown the cynical familiarity common among accomplices. No feature of their situation was too shameful to discuss. With an ominous frankness they gave everything its proper name and, as they described it to themselves, looked reality in the face.

During February winter had appeared finished. Then Mother March arrived, shaking out her white cloak with its loose lining, and storm after storm laid thick blankets of snow over the ground. Stillness and a sharp frost followed. A six-inch covering of ice closed over the fjord and remained unbroken for a long while.
Near the end of the month, one evening after tea, Fennimore sat by herself in the parlour, waiting.

Light filled the room. The piano was open and its candles burning; the lamp's silk shade had been removed. Gilt mouldings glittered, and the wall pictures seemed to project watchfully into the room. Moved from the windows to the writing desk, the hyacinths formed a mass of subtle colour. Their sharp perfume filled the air, seeming cool because it was so pure. Inside the stove the fire crackled pleasantly and softly.

Fennimore paced back and forth, appearing to balance along a deep-red line in the carpet. She wore a slightly outmoded black silk gown. Heavy embroidery weighted its hem, which swung and trailed first on one side and then on the other with each of her steps.

She hummed, both hands holding the necklace of large, pale-amber beads at her throat. Whenever her feet strayed on the red line the humming ceased, but her hands maintained their grip. Perhaps she was consulting a private omen: if she could complete a certain number of journeys up and down without leaving the stripe or releasing the beads, Niels would arrive.

He had come that morning as Erik departed and remained until late afternoon. Before he left he had promised to return once the moon rose and provided enough light to distinguish the openings in the fjord's ice.
Whatever sign she wanted had been granted. Fennimore left the carpet stripe and approached the window.

There seemed little prospect of moonlight. The heavens were pitch-black, and out on the grey-blue fjord it must be darker still than on the snow-covered ground. Perhaps he would be wise not to try crossing. With a resigned sigh she sat at the piano, then rose again to check the time. Returning, she purposefully opened a large music volume in front of her. But she played nothing, only turning pages without attention, immersed in thought.

Perhaps even now he was on the farther bank buckling his skates. He could arrive in a moment! She could see him distinctly, breathing a little hard from the crossing, blinking at the brightness after the outdoor dark. Cold air would come in with him, and tiny shining droplets would cover his beard. Then he would speak—what would he say to her?
She smiled, lowering her eyes to her own dress.
The moon still refused to show itself.

Back at the window she gazed into the blackness until little white sparks and rainbow rings began dancing before her eyes. They were only an uncertain shimmer. She wished they would become real fireworks outside: rockets rising in immense curves and turning into little snakes that drilled into heaven before flickering out; or an enormous pale globe suspended trembling above her, slowly dissolving into a shower of multicoloured stars. Look, look! Look at them! Softly rounded like a curtsy, like golden rain bending its knees. Goodbye! Goodbye! The last one had gone. Oh, if he would only arrive! She didn't want to play. At that thought she turned to the piano, struck an octave violently, and held it until the sound entirely faded. Then she repeated it, again and again. She didn't want music, she didn't. Dancing was what she wanted! Closing her eyes briefly, she imagined spinning through an immense ballroom of red, white, and gold. How delicious to have danced, to be flushed and exhausted, drinking champagne! Then she abruptly recalled making champagne with a schoolfriend out of soda water and eau de cologne, and how ill drinking it had made them.
She drew herself upright and crossed the floor, instinctively straightening her gown as though a dance had just ended.
“Time to show some sense!” she announced, fetched her embroidery, and took a large chair beside the lamp.

No sewing followed. Her hands dropped into her lap. With small, idle shifts she soon fitted herself snugly into the chair's hollows, resting her face against one hand and drawing the skirt about her feet.

She wondered whether other married women resembled her, whether they too had chosen wrongly, been miserable, and afterward loved another man. One by one she considered the women she knew in Fjordby. Then Mrs. Boye came to mind. Niels had spoken of her, and she remained an exasperating mystery to Fennimore, a woman she hated and by whom she felt humiliated.
Once Erik, too, had admitted to having been desperately in love with Mrs. Boye.
Oh, to know every last thing about her!
The image of Mrs. Boye's latest husband made her laugh.

Throughout these wandering thoughts she kept listening and yearning for Niels, picturing him approaching, endlessly approaching over the frozen water. She never guessed that during the past two hours a tiny dark speck had been crossing the snow-covered meadows with quite another message than the one she awaited from beyond the fjord. The speck was simply a man wearing homespun and oiled boots. Now he knocked at the kitchen window, startling the maid.

Trine entered with what she called a letter. Fennimore took it: a telegram. Without agitation she handed back the receipt and sent the maid away. There was no reason to worry; lately Erik had often sent telegrams announcing that he would bring a guest or two home the next day.
She began reading it.
All at once her colour vanished. She sprang from the chair into the room's centre, her eyes fixed on the doorway in terrified expectation.

She would not admit it, dared not allow it inside. In a leap she reached the door, drove her shoulder against it, and twisted the key until it bit into her palm. No effort would make it turn. Her hand fell uselessly. Then she recalled that the thing was not here: it was far away, in an unfamiliar house.
Trembling began. Her legs could no longer hold her, and she slipped down the door onto the carpet.

Erik had died. The horses bolted, the carriage overturned on a street corner, and he was flung headfirst against a wall. His skull was broken; now he lay dead in Aalborg. That was what had occurred, most of it stated in the telegram. Only the tutor in the white neckcloth, the one called the Arab, had been riding beside him. The Arab had sent the message.
She huddled on the floor, moaning weakly, both hands flattened against the carpet. Her eyes stared emptily at nothing as her body rocked helplessly backward and forward.

A moment earlier fragrance and brightness had surrounded her. Try as she might, she could not immediately expel them from her mind to make room for grief and remorse in their pitch-black night. It wasn't her fault that brilliant, erratic flashes of love's joy and pleasure still haunted her; that fierce, senseless wishes fought their way through the turmoil, reaching for oblivion's happiness, or trying with one mad wrench to halt fortune's turning wheel.
Soon enough, though, that ended.

Black flocks of thoughts swooped from every side like ravens, drawn to the carcass of her happiness. Beak after beak struck it while the warmth of living still remained. They ripped and slashed until it was hideous, unrecognizable, nothing left but a corpse of disgust and terror.

She got up and moved around, leaning on tables and chairs like an invalid. Desperately she searched for the thinnest thread of help, perhaps a kind glance, a sympathetic hand. Nothing answered except the staring family portraits, strangers who had witnessed her degradation and her sin: drowsy old men, tight-lipped matrons, and their perpetual little goblin child, the girl with enormous round eyes and a bulging brow. This foreign furniture had finally gathered memories enough: that table, this chair, the footrest embroidered with a black poodle, the curtain resembling a dressing gown. She had steeped them all in memories of adultery, and now they vomited those memories back, hurling them after her. How dreadful to be imprisoned with these ghosts of wrongdoing, imprisoned with herself. She recoiled from herself, pointed accusingly at herself, at the disgraced Fennimore cowering below her. She pulled her skirts clear of that woman's begging fingers. Pity? No pity existed! How could it exist before those dead eyes in the distant town? Death had glazed them and given them sight: they saw how she had dragged his honour through dirt, lied against his mouth, betrayed him against his heart.

Those dead eyes seemed fastened upon her. Their source was invisible, yet she felt them follow, sliding over her body like a pair of icy beams. Looking down, she saw each carpet thread and every stitch in the footrests with unnatural distinctness in the fierce light. Something seemed to circle her on a dead man's feet. Its touch against her dress was so real that she screamed and leapt aside. But it appeared in front of her, like hands yet unlike hands, reaching slowly, triumphantly, mockingly for her heart, that miraculous piece of treachery, that yellow pearl of fraud! She backed away until she struck the table, but still it reached her. Her breast afforded no defence: it grasped through flesh and skin.... Terror almost killed her. Helpless, bending backward across the tabletop, she felt every nerve tighten, her eyes staring as if they were being slaughtered inside their sockets.
That visitation, too, passed.

She glanced about like someone hunted, then dropped to her knees and prayed at length. Confession and repentance poured out wildly, without restraint, rising into the same fanatical hatred of self that makes a nun whip her uncovered flesh. Eagerly she hunted the most abject phrases, intoxicating herself with abasement, with a humility thirsty for further humiliation.
Finally she stood up. Her chest rose and fell fiercely. A trace of brightness touched her pale cheeks, which seemed to have filled out while she prayed.

She surveyed the room as if making a wordless pledge. Then she entered the next room and closed the door. Pausing briefly to adjust to the dark, she felt her way towards the door of the glassed-in veranda and stepped through.

More light reached the veranda. The moon was up, shining through the tightly clustered frost crystals on the windows. Ordinary panes admitted a yellow glow; the coloured squares bordering them let through blue and red.
With her palm she thawed an opening in the frost, then carefully dried the wet patch with her handkerchief.
Nobody could yet be seen upon the frozen fjord.

She began slowly pacing inside the glass enclosure. Its only furnishing was a bentwood-and-cane couch littered with dry ivy leaves fallen from the climbing stems above. As she passed, the displaced air stirred them into a faint rustle. Occasionally her hem caught a leaf on the floor and dragged it scratching across the boards.
Back and forth she kept her desolate vigil, arms crossed tightly over her chest, refusing to yield to the chill.
He appeared at last.
She jerked the door open and went out onto the frozen snow in her light shoes. She spared herself nothing; she could have walked barefoot to meet him.
Seeing a dark figure against the snow, Niels reduced his speed and approached the bank with cautious, uncertain strokes.

His furtive shape seemed seared into her sight. Each known gesture, each familiar feature, looked like a brazen affront, a boast about shameful secrets. Hatred shook her. Curses swelled within her heart, and she could barely hold her fury in check.
“It’s me out here!” she called mockingly. “Fennimore, the whore!”
“For heaven's sake, darling, what's wrong?” he asked in astonishment when only a few feet separated them.
“Erik is dead.”
“Dead! When did it happen?” To avoid toppling, he stepped off the ice, skates and all, into the snow. “Oh, tell me!” He moved urgently nearer.
They stood close now. She had to check the impulse to smash her fist into his pale, contorted face.
“You'll hear, don't worry,” she cried. “As I told you, he's dead. The horses ran away in Aalborg and his head was crushed, while you and I were here betraying him.”

“How dreadful!” Niels groaned, clutching his temples. “Who could have imagined it—oh, Fennimore, if only we'd stayed true to him! Poor Erik, Erik! If only it had been me instead!” He sobbed loudly, twisting in anguish.
“Niels Lyhne, I hate you!”

“What do either of us matter now?” he moaned. “If we could bring him back! Poor Fennimore!” A different feeling moved him. “Forget about me. You say you hate me? You have every reason.” Suddenly he straightened. “Let's go inside. I don't know what I'm saying. Who sent the telegram, did you tell me?”

“Inside!” His disregard of her hatred infuriated Fennimore. “Inside that house! You'll never put your cowardly, contemptible foot through its door again. How dare you even think it, you miserable creature, you lying dog who crept in and robbed your friend of his honour because he hadn't hidden it securely enough! You stole it in front of him because he trusted your honesty, you thief in his own home!”

“Quiet, be quiet. Have you lost your mind? What's got into you! How can you talk like this?” He seized her arm, pulled her firmly towards him, and stared into her face, bewildered. More softly he said, “Try to recover yourself, child. Flinging filthy insults won't repair anything.”
She tore free so violently that he lurched and nearly fell from his already precarious footing.

“Don't you hear me saying I hate you!” Her voice rose to a shriek. “Isn't there a scrap of a decent man's understanding left in you to grasp that! How blind I was to love you, a creature cobbled together from falsehoods, when beside me stood a man ten thousand times your better. I'll despise and hate you until I die. Before you arrived I was honourable; I'd never done an evil thing. Then you brought your poetry and nonsense and lied me down into the dirt beside you. How had I injured you, that you couldn't leave me untouched, me of all women, who ought to have been sacred to you! Now I must live each day with this disgrace staining my soul. However vile a person I encounter, I'll know myself more vile. You've poisoned every memory of my girlhood. What unspoilt, good thing remains for me to remember! You've infected it all. He isn't the only one dead: every bright and good thing we shared has died and rotted as well. Oh God, is it just that after everything you've done I can't even revenge myself? Restore my honour, Niels Lyhne, make me clean and good again! No, no—but surely it should be possible to torture you until you undo your deed. Can your lies undo it? Don't stand shrinking there behind your inability. I want you suffering before my eyes, twisting in misery, pain, and despair. God, make him miserable, don't let him rob me of vengeance too! Leave, you wretch, leave! I reject you, but know that I'll drag you through every torment my hatred can summon onto your head.”
Her arms had reached towards him in a threatening gesture. Now she turned back into the house, shutting the veranda door with a quiet rattle.

Niels gazed after her, astonished, scarcely believing. Her white, vindictive face seemed still before him, so peculiarly coarse and mean in spirit, stripped of every fine contour, as though a savage hand had ploughed through its beauty.

He cautiously picked his way uncertainly back to the ice and began skating slowly towards the fjord's mouth, moonlight ahead and wind behind. As his thoughts drew him away from his surroundings he gathered speed. Splinters sprayed from his blades and clattered over the smooth ice, travelling with him on the strengthening, freezing wind.

So this was the outcome! This was his rescue of a woman's soul, his uplifting of her, his gift of happiness! And how beautiful his conduct towards his dead friend, his childhood companion, for whom he would have sacrificed his future, his existence, everything! What a rescuer and sacrificer he was! Let earth and heaven admire a man keeping his life spotless on honour's summit, lest any blemish darken the Idea he served and had been appointed to spread.

Probably that, too, was simply another grandiose fantasy: that his wretched little existence could stain the Idea's sun. Good God, these magnificent assessments of himself were habitual, bred into his very bones. If nothing greater was possible, at least he must become Judas, solemnly naming himself Iscariot in imposing despair. That had an impressive sound. Would he never stop acting as though he were the Idea's accountable minister, seated on its privy council and receiving all humanity's affairs directly! Would he never learn plain, unpretentious barrack duty in its service, an ordinary soldier of a decidedly low rank?
Fires glowed red out on the ice. He passed close enough for an enormous shadow to spring from his feet, swing ahead of him, and instantly vanish.

He thought about Erik and what sort of friendship he had given him. He, of all people! His childhood recollections wrung their hands at him; his youthful hopes covered their faces and cried. His entire past watched him go with a long, accusing gaze. He had sold it all for a love as petty and poor as himself. That love _had_ contained greatness, but he had betrayed that as well.

Where could he escape these undertakings that always landed in a ditch? His life had consisted of nothing else, and would never produce anything else. He knew it with such certainty that the thought of all that wasted effort sickened him. With his whole being he wished to run from this senseless destiny. If only the ice would part beneath his skates and finish everything in one gasp, one convulsion in the freezing water!

Worn out, he halted and turned around. The moon had set. The fjord lay long and black between snowy hills. He began fighting his way home into the wind, now blowing hard. Tired, he moved nearer land for the hills' shelter. But as he struggled forward he reached an opening that gusts sweeping down those hills had made in the ice. Beneath him the thin, flexible covering cracked and began to give way.
Despite everything, how freely he breathed on reaching solid ice once more! Fear had almost erased his fatigue, and he drove his skates onward with renewed strength.

While he battled outside, Fennimore remained in the bright room, frustrated and unhappy. Her revenge seemed stolen from her. She could hardly say what she had expected, only that it had been entirely different. She had envisioned something grand and overwhelming, something of swords and scarlet flames—or not exactly that, but something sweeping her upward to a throne. Instead it had dwindled into pettiness and insignificance. She had felt like an ordinary quarrelling woman, rather than someone pronouncing a curse....
She had, after all, learnt a thing or two from Niels.
Early the next morning, while Niels still slept under the weight of exhaustion, Fennimore departed from the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: For the better part of two years Niels Lyhne had wandered about on the Continent.

He was very alone, with no family or close friend to anchor him. And yet a greater loneliness surrounded him still; for however forsaken a man may feel when there is no single place on earth his affections can cling to — no place he can bless when his heart overflows, no place he can long for when longing spreads its wings — there is no existence so lonely that he is utterly alone, provided he can see the steady bright star of a life goal shining overhead. But Niels Lyhne had no such star. He did not know what to do with himself or with his gifts. It was all very well to have talent, if only he could put it to use, but he moved through the world like a painter without hands. How he envied the people, great and small, who whenever they reached out into life found a handle they could grip; he could never find any handle at all. It seemed he could do nothing but sing the old romantic songs over again, and in truth that was all he had done so far. His talent felt like something set apart inside him, a quiet Pompeii, or a harp that had to be taken out of its corner. It was not everywhere in him, did not run down the street with him or tingle in his fingertips — not in the least. His talent had no hold on him. Sometimes he felt he had been born half a century too late; sometimes he felt he had arrived much too early. His talent was rooted in something from the past; it could draw no nourishment from his opinions, his convictions, his sympathies, could not absorb them and give them form. The two elements seemed forever to slip apart like water and oil, which can be shaken together but will never mix, never become one.

As he gradually came to see this, he sank into a deep dejection and began to regard himself and his whole past with an ironic, suspicious eye. Something must be wrong with him, he told himself — something incurably wrong in the very marrow of his being; for surely a man ought to be able to fuse the differing elements of his own nature, that much he firmly believed.
This was the state of his mind when he settled down, in September of the second year of his exile, on the shores of Lake Garda, in the little town of Riva.

Not long afterward, the whole region was cordoned off by troubles that brought travel to a halt and kept strangers away. Cholera had broken out near Venice, and to the south in Desenzano, and to the north around the Trentino. Under these circumstances Riva was anything but lively: the hotels had emptied at the first rumor, and tourists heading for Italy took another route.
Naturally the few who remained drew all the more closely together.

The most striking person among them was a famous opera singer, whose real name was Madame Odéro. Her stage name was far more celebrated than that. She and her companion, Niels, and a deaf doctor from Vienna were the only guests at the Golden Sun, the leading hotel in town.

Niels felt strongly drawn to her, and she in turn responded to that warmth of manner which is often found in people who are at odds with themselves and therefore feel the need to put their relations with others on solid footing.

Madame Odéro had been living in Riva for nearly seven months, trying to recover, through complete rest, from the aftereffects of a throat ailment that had threatened her voice. Her physician had told her to abstain for a full year from singing and, in order to avoid temptation, from all music. Only when the year was up would he allow her to try her voice again, and if no weariness followed she might consider herself cured.

Niels came to exert a kind of civilizing influence over Madame Odéro, who was a fiery, passionate nature with no fine shades. It had been a terrible sentence to her when she was condemned to live a whole year without applause and adoration, and at first she had been desperate, staring in horror at the twelve months stretching before her like a deep black grave into which she was being lowered; but everyone seemed to think it was unavoidable, and one fine morning she had suddenly fled to Riva. She could easily have chosen a livelier and more fashionable place, but that was precisely what she wanted to avoid. She felt ashamed, as though she had been marked with an outward visible blemish, imagining that people pitied her for this infirmity and discussed her among themselves. So she had shunned all society in her new town and lived almost entirely in her rooms, where from time to time she took revenge on the doors when her voluntary confinement became unbearable. Now that everyone else had gone, she emerged again and came to know Niels Lyhne — for she was not afraid of people taken one at a time.

No one needed long in Madame Odéro’s company to find out whether she liked him or not, for she showed it plainly enough. What she let Niels Lyhne see was very encouraging, and they had not been alone many days in the magnificent hotel garden — with its pomegranates and myrtles, its arbors of flowering oleanders and its marvelous view — before they were on very friendly terms.

They were not in love with each other, or if they were, it was not serious. It was one of those vague, pleasant intimacies that sometimes grow up between men and women past the age of early youth, when nature flares up and yearns toward an unknown bliss. It is a kind of waning summer, in which people stroll decorously side by side, gather themselves into graceful bouquets, each caressing himself with the other’s hand and admiring himself through the other’s eyes. They take out all their store of pretty secrets, all those exquisite useless trifles people collect like bric-à-brac of the soul, pass them from hand to hand, turn them around and hold them up, seeking the most artistic light, comparing and analyzing.

Of course, such Sunday friendships are only possible when life moves at a leisurely pace, and here by the quiet lake these two had plenty of time. Niels began by draping Madame Odéro in a becoming robe of melancholy. At first she was several times on the verge of tearing the whole thing off and revealing herself as the barbarian she was, but when she discovered that she could wear the drapery to patrician effect, she took her melancholy as a role. She not only stopped slamming doors but began to search out the moods and emotions in herself that might suit her new pose. It was astonishing how she came to realize that she had actually known herself very little before. Her life had been too eventful and exciting to give her time to explore herself, and besides, she was only now approaching the age when women who have lived much in the world and seen much begin to collect their memories, to look back at themselves and assemble a past.
From this beginning their intimacy developed quickly and unmistakably until each of them had become indispensable to the other. Neither led more than a half-hearted existence without the other.

Then it happened one morning, as Niels was setting out for a sail, that he heard Madame Odéro singing in the garden. His first impulse was to turn back and scold her, but before he could make up his mind the boat had carried him out of hearing; the wind tempted him to a trip to Limone, and he meant to be back by midday. So he sailed on.

Madame Odéro had come down into the garden earlier than usual. The fresh fragrance in the air, the round waves rising and falling clear and bright as glass beneath the garden wall, and all that glory of color everywhere — blue lake and sun-scorched mountains, white sails flitting across the water and red flowers arching over her head — all of this, together with a dream she could not shake, which went on throbbing against her heart.... She could not stay silent; she had to join in all this life.
So she sang.

Fuller and fuller the exultant notes of her voice rose. She was intoxicated with its beauty, she trembled in a voluptuous sense of its power; and she went on, unable to stop, for she was being carried blissfully along on wonderful dreams of triumphs to come.
No weariness followed. She could leave — leave at once, shake off the nothingness of the past months, come out of hiding and live!
By midday everything was ready for her departure.

Then, just as the carriages drew up to the door, she remembered Niels Lyhne. She dug down into her pocket for a shabby little notebook and scribbled it full of farewells to him, for the pages were so small that each could hold only three or four words. This she tucked into an envelope for him and departed.
