When Niels came back in the late afternoon, having been held up by the sanitary police in Limone, she had long since reached Mori and taken the train.

He was not surprised, only sorry, and not at all angry. He could even smile resignedly at this fresh hostile thrust of fate. But in the evening, when he sat in the empty moonlit garden telling the innkeeper’s little boy the story of the princess who found her wings again and flew away from her lover back to the land of fairies, he was seized by an unbearable longing for Lönborggaard. He yearned to feel something close around him like a home and hold him fast, no matter how. He could not endure the indifference of life any longer, could not bear being cast off and thrown back on himself again and again. No home on earth, no God in heaven, no goal out there in the future! He would at least have a home. He would make it his own by loving everything there, big and small, every rock, every tree, the living and the lifeless; he would portion out his heart to all of it so that it could never cast him off again.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Niels Lyhne had spent about a year at Lönborggaard, running the farm to the limits of his knowledge and of what the old steward would permit. He had lowered his shield, erased his coat of arms, and withdrawn. Humanity must manage without him. He had discovered the satisfaction of bodily labour: watching the heap grow beneath his hands, finishing a task and knowing it really _was_ finished. When he left exhausted, the energy he had spent remained behind in the work. It would endure, untouched by doubts eating into it overnight or by the breath of next morning's criticism scattering it. Farming had no stones of Sisyphus to keep rolling back.

And how pleasant, after working himself tired, to lie down and recover strength through sleep, then spend that strength afresh, as steadily as night follows day. No whims of the mind interrupted him; he need not treat himself like a tuned guitar whose pegs kept slipping.

In a quiet fashion he was truly content. Often, like his father before him, he sat on a stile or a boundary marker, looking across golden grain or oats bowed under their own weight, sunk in an odd, plant-like reverie.
He had not yet sought out neighbouring households, apart from Councillor Skinnerup's in Varde, where his visits were quite frequent.

The Skinnerups had moved there before his father's death. Since the Councillor and Lyhne had been university friends, their families had often met. Gentle and bald, with sharp features and kindly eyes, Skinnerup was now widowed. His four girls more than filled the house, however; they ranged from twelve to seventeen.

The Councillor was widely read, and Niels liked discussing matters of art and literature with him. Learning manual work had hardly transformed him overnight into a rustic, after all. Sometimes he found the care demanded by these conversations almost comically excessive. Any comparison between foreign and Danish writing, indeed any comparison of Denmark with anything beyond it, required extraordinary caution. That caution was essential: mild though he was, the Councillor belonged to the ferocious patriots one occasionally met in those years. Reluctantly he might concede that Denmark was not the foremost world power. Once that admission had been made, though, he would yield not another particle that could place his country, or anything associated with it, anywhere except first.

There was a further attraction in these discussions, which Niels initially sensed only dimly, without conscious acknowledgment. Gerda, seventeen, followed his speeches with delighted, admiring eyes. Somehow she always contrived to be there when he called. Her attention was so ardent that he often noticed her cheeks flush with happiness at some remark she found particularly beautiful.

Without knowing it he had become this girl's ideal. At first this was chiefly because he often rode into town in a grey cloak with a strikingly foreign, romantic cut. Next came his habit of saying Milano rather than Milan; finally, he was alone in the world and looked rather sad. Certainly there were many respects in which he differed from everyone else in Varde, and in Ringkjöbing as well.

One hot day that summer, Niels walked along the little street behind the Councillor's garden. Sunshine blazed on the small brick-red houses. Mats hung over the sides of the ships in the sound, preventing tar from melting out of their seams. Everywhere doors and windows stood open in pursuit of a coolness nowhere to be found. Through doorways came the sound of children reciting lessons, their voices blending with the bees' humming in the gardens. Sparrows travelled silently from tree to tree, a flock rising all together and settling all together.

He entered a small house immediately behind the garden. The woman went to fetch her husband from next door, leaving Niels in an immaculate little room scented with gillyflowers and newly pressed linen.

After inspecting the pictures, the pair of dogs on the dresser, and the shells decorating the sewing-box lid, he approached the open window. Gerda's voice reached him. Only a few steps away, the Councillor's four daughters stood on the grass used for bleaching linen.
Screened by balsamines and the other plants on the sill, he settled in to watch as well as listen.

Clearly an argument was in progress, with the three younger girls united against Gerda. Each held a whip of yellow, lemon-coloured twigs. The youngest had bent several of hers into hoops, bound them with red bark, and arranged them on her head as a turban.
The youngest girl held the floor.
“She thinks he's like the Themistocles on the study stove,” she informed her accomplices, rolling her eyes upward with a look of worship.

“Oh, nonsense,” said the middle sister, a pert young thing confirmed only that spring. “Do you imagine Themistocles stooped?” She copied the slight rounding of Niels Lyhne's shoulders. “Themistocles! Hardly!”
The twelve-year-old quoted: “There's such manliness in his expression; he's truly a man!”
“Him!” the middle sister exclaimed again. “He actually sprinkles himself with eau de cologne. His gloves were lying about the other day, positively stinking of millefleur.”
“_Every_ perfection!” sighed the twelve-year-old, falling backward as though her feelings were too much for her.
They directed their observations at one another, pretending Gerda wasn't there. A little apart, she blushed deeply and prodded the soil with her yellow wand. Then, suddenly, she raised her head.
“You're two shameless little hussies,” she said, “talking that way about somebody too good even to notice you.”
“But surely he's _only_ human,” the oldest of the three objected gently, pretending to seek agreement.
“No, he is _nothing_ of the sort.”
Her sister went on as though she hadn't heard: “And _surely_ there must be faults in him.”
“No!”
“But Gerda, darling, you _know_ he never attends church.”
“Why would he need to? He knows _far_ more than the pastor does.”
“Unfortunately, though, Gerda, he doesn't believe in any God _at all_.”
“Then rest assured, my dear, that if he doesn't, his reasons are _excellent_ ones.”
“Gerda, how could you possibly say that!”
The middle sister interrupted: “One might almost imagine—”
“Might almost imagine what?” Gerda demanded sharply.
“Nothing, absolutely nothing. Don't bite my head off!” Her sister suddenly assumed a very humble manner.
“Tell me immediately what you were going to say!”
“No, no, no, no, no. Surely I may keep quiet if that's what I choose.”
She and the youngest walked off arm in arm, each clasping the other's shoulder in sisterly harmony. The oldest followed, stalking away with an air of indignation.
Alone, Gerda stared defiantly ahead and slashed at the empty air with her yellow twig.
A brief hush followed. Then, from the garden's far end, the youngest sister's thin voice rose in song:
“_You ask me, my lad, What I want with the withered flower_—”

Niels understood the taunt exactly. He had lately given Gerda a book containing a dried vine leaf from the garden in Verona where Juliet's tomb stood. He almost laughed aloud. Just then the woman returned with her husband, found at last, and he had to explain the carpentry commission that had brought him there.
After that day Niels paid closer attention to Gerda. Each encounter made him more aware of her sweetness and delicacy. Increasingly, as time passed, his mind returned to this trusting young girl.

She was lovely in a tender, touching way that almost made one want to cry. Her figure, only beginning to mature, still had a child's rounded shape, lending innocence to its abundant womanliness. Her little softly shaped hands were shedding the pinkness of adolescence. They showed none of the fidgeting, inquisitive nervousness so common at her age. A sturdy little neck supported cheeks curved in full, generous lines. Her low brow was dreamy and feminine; large ideas were strangers there and almost seemed painful when they arrived, drawing her thick eyebrows together. And her eyes: what blue depths they held, though deep only like clear lakes whose bottoms remain visible. A happy smile slept in their gentle corners beneath lids lifted with slow astonishment. This was little Gerda, pink and white and fair, her short, bright hair modestly drawn together into a knot.

Niels and Gerda talked often, and his love increased with every conversation. His affection remained candid, open, chivalrous, until one day the air between them changed. Something glimmered there too weightless to be called sensuality, yet born of the senses: the impulse that sends eyes, lips, and hands towards someone the heart cannot draw close enough. On another day, not very long afterward, because she was so young and because he felt so certain she loved him, Niels spoke to Gerda's father. Her father consented, and Gerda consented too.
Their wedding took place in spring.
To Niels Lyhne, existence now seemed marvellously clear and uncomplicated. Living had become simple, and happiness seemed as near at hand and as easily obtained as the air he breathed.

He loved his young wife with all the sensitivity of mind and feeling, all the deep, expansive tenderness, of a man who understands how love can fall and trusts its ability to rise. How carefully he guarded the young soul leaning towards him in limitless confidence, pressing affectionately against him in absolute faith that he could bring her only good, as the parable's little ewe lamb must have trusted its shepherd while feeding from his hand and drinking from his cup! He could not bear to deprive her of God, or banish those white companies of angels who sing their way through heaven by day and descend at evening, spreading wings from bed to bed. Faithfully they watch, building a protective barrier of unseen brightness within the dark. He dreaded setting his own graver, imageless understanding of existence between her and the sky's soft blue, leaving her troubled and abandoned.

She insisted on a different course. She wanted to share absolutely everything with him; nowhere on earth or in heaven should their paths divide. Whatever objections he raised to restrain her, she answered with the Moabite woman's stubborn resolve, if not her actual words: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.

So he set himself seriously to teaching her. Gods, he explained, were human creations, and like everything people create they could not last for ever. One generation of gods must give way to another, since humanity continually develops and outgrows its own ideals. Suppose the best and greatest people could no longer offer a god the richest gifts of their minds; suppose that god no longer drew illumination from humanity, but had to shine by some quality of his own; suppose he stopped developing and hardened inside the historical plaster of dogma. He would be a god no longer, merely an idol. Thus Judaism had been right against Baal and Astarte, and Christianity right against Judaism: an idol amounts to nothing in the world. Humanity had progressed from one god to the next. Christ could therefore look back towards the older God and say He had come not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, while also indicating an ideal beyond Himself, higher still, in those mysterious words concerning the unforgivable sin, the sin against the Holy Ghost.

He explained further that believing in a personal God who arranges everything for the best, dispensing punishment and reward after death, was an escape from life's hard facts, a helpless effort to blunt its arbitrariness. Such belief, he said, inevitably dulled compassion and weakened the impulse to spend every effort relieving suffering. People could comfort themselves by imagining that pain in this short earthly existence prepared the sufferer for endless glory and delight.

He emphasized the independence and strength humanity would acquire through confidence in itself. Each individual would try to harmonize life with what, in the finest moments, seemed highest within, rather than looking outside for a ruling divinity. He presented his conviction as beautifully and blessedly as possible. Yet he did not hide how crushingly sad, how devoid of consolation, atheism's truth might appear in grief beside the lovely old dream of a guiding, governing Father in Heaven. She showed courage nevertheless. Many of his teachings, often those he least expected to disturb her, shook her to the soul's centre. But trust knew no limits for her. Love carried her alongside him out of every heaven; she believed through loving. Eventually the unfamiliar thoughts became familiar, a home to live in. Then she grew fiercely intolerant and fanatical, as young converts who passionately love their teacher so often do. Niels frequently reproved her, but this one point escaped her understanding: if their belief was true, how could everyone else's fail to be dreadful and blameworthy?
They spent three happy years together. Much of their happiness shone out of a baby's face, the face of the son born during their second year of marriage.

Happiness generally brings out people's goodness. Niels worked sincerely to make their shared life lovely, generous, and useful, allowing their souls to keep growing towards the human ideal they both accepted. But he no longer imagined bearing its banner before the world; following it satisfied him. Sometimes he brought out an old unfinished work and wondered whether those graceful, carefully fashioned pieces could really have come from him. Reading his own verses always moved him to tears. Yet nothing could have induced him to exchange places with the unfortunate man who had written them.
Then, suddenly that spring, Gerda became ill, and recovery did not come.

Early one morning, her last, Niels sat watching beside her. The approaching sunrise tinted the white blinds red, although the light entering at their sides remained blue. Blue shadows lay in the coverlet's folds and beneath Gerda's pale, thin hands, clasped upon the sheet. Her cap had fallen away. With her head far back in the pillow, her features, sharpened and made delicate by pain, looked unfamiliar, strangely distinguished. Her lips moved as though she wished to wet them. Niels reached for a glass containing a dark-red drink, but a slight movement of her head refused it. Suddenly she faced him, studying his sorrowful expression with anxious attention. The grief written there, the despair he could not disguise, slowly changed her uneasy suspicion into dreadful certainty.
She tried to sit up and failed.
He quickly leaned towards her, and she seized his hand.
“Am I dying?” she asked, making her faint voice still quieter, as if the words were unbearable to say.
He could do nothing but meet her gaze, drawing a deep breath that came out in a moan.
Terrified, Gerda gripped his hand and turned towards him with all her strength. “I'm afraid to,” she said.

He sank to his knees beside the bed and slipped his arm under the pillow, almost holding her against his chest. Tears ran down his face so continuously that he could scarcely see her. He raised her hand, together with an edge of the sheet, to wipe his eyes. Then he gained command of his voice. “Tell me everything, darling Gerda. Don't worry about me. Do you want the pastor?” Doubt sounded in the question; he could barely believe that was her wish.
She offered no answer. Closing her eyes, she withdrew her head slightly, as though wishing to be alone inside her thoughts.
Several minutes went by. Beneath the windows a blackbird gave a soft, lingering whistle. Another answered, then another, sending a whole succession of flute notes through the silent room.
She looked at him again. “If you could come with me,” she said, leaning harder against the pillow on his arm. It was a caress, and he understood it. “If you were coming too! But by myself!”

Weakly she pulled his hand towards her, then released it. “I'm too afraid.” Fright filled her eyes. “You have to bring him, Niels. I dare not go up there all alone like this. We never imagined I'd be first to die; you always went ahead. Yes, I know, but what if we were mistaken after all? We _could_ be mistaken, couldn't we, Niels? You don't believe so, but surely it would be odd if _everyone_ were wrong and there were nothing whatsoever—all those great churches, and the bells when somebody's buried. I've always loved the bells so much.” She lay without moving, as though listening and already hearing them.

“Everything can't simply end when we die, Niels. You can't sense it while you're well. Because we're weak and everything seems to disappear, you imagine it must destroy us entirely. But only the outside world fades; inside there's just as much soul as ever. It's still there, Niels. I have everything within me, everything I've received, the same limitless world, only quieter, more alone with myself, like closing one's eyes. It's like a candle being carried away from you into darkness, Niels, farther into darkness. To you the flame grows smaller and smaller until it vanishes. But where it is, far off, it still gives light. I always imagined becoming such an old, old woman, remaining here with all of you. Now they won't allow it. They're taking me out of my home and making me travel alone. I'm afraid God rules wherever I'm going, Niels, and our earthly cleverness means nothing to Him. He insists on His own way, nothing else. Yet somehow all that belongs to Him feels so remote from me. I haven't been terribly wicked, have I? But that isn't it.... Please bring the pastor; I need him so much.”
Niels rose immediately and went out to fetch the pastor. He was thankful that this request had come before the very last moment.
When the pastor arrived, he and Gerda were left together.

He was a handsome man of middle age, with large brown eyes and regular, finely shaped features. Naturally he knew Niels Lyhne's position towards the church. From time to time people had also reported hostile remarks born of Gerda's fervour. Yet addressing her as a heathen or renegade never entered his mind. He knew perfectly well that love alone had drawn her away, and understood why, now love could accompany her no farther, she wished to be reconciled with the God of her earlier life. So he tried to awaken sleeping memories in their conversation, reading the Gospel passages and hymns he thought she would recognize most readily.
His judgment proved right.

The familiar words rang solemnly within her, like bells on Christmas morning. Instantly she saw the country where imagination first makes its home, where Joseph dreamed and David sang, where the ladder rises from earth into heaven. Fig and mulberry trees grew there. In the morning haze the Jordan glittered, pure silver; Jerusalem stood sombre and red beneath the declining sun. Over Bethlehem, though, night was always magnificent, its deep blue dome filled with great stars. How powerfully her childhood faith returned! Again she was the little girl holding her mother's hand on the way to church, sitting there cold and wondering why people committed so many sins. Then the Sermon on the Mount, with its lofty language, raised her to adulthood once more. As the pastor spoke of baptism's holy mystery and holy communion, she lay like a sinner cast down before God. Finally the true desire stirred: humble kneeling before the almighty Judge, bitter repentant tears before the betrayed, insulted, suffering God, and the desire, both meek and daring, to enter through bread and wine a new covenant with the hidden God.
The pastor withdrew. He returned around midday and administered the sacrament to her.

Her strength dwindled in uneven flickers. Still, when evening darkened and Niels held her one last time to take his leave before death's shadows drew too close, her mind was clear. The love that had supplied his life's purest happiness no longer shone in her eyes. She belonged to him no more. Her wings were already growing, and all her longing went to God.
Death came at midnight.

Bleak months followed. Time expanded into something immense and hostile. Each day stretched as an endless waste of vacancy, each night became a torment of recollection. Not until summer was nearly finished did grief's foaming, headlong torrent wear a channel through his soul, settling into a heavy, murmuring river of sadness and desire.

One day he came back from the fields to discover his small son desperately ill. For several days the child had seemed unwell and had slept restlessly, but nobody expected anything grave. Now he lay in his little bed, shivering and burning by turns, moaning in pain.
They sent the carriage to Varde immediately for medical help. No doctor was at home, however, and it waited for hours. Bedtime arrived without its return.

Beside his son's cot Niels waited, sending someone every half-hour, sometimes more often, to watch and listen for wheels. A rider went out to meet the carriage too, but saw no sign of it and continued all the way into Varde.

The wait for assistance that never arrived made witnessing the child's torment still harder. The illness advanced swiftly. Around eleven the first fit of convulsions began; afterward the seizures returned repeatedly, with less and less time between them.
Shortly after one the rider reappeared. They could expect no carriage for several more hours, he reported: when he left town, not one of the doctors had returned.

Niels could hold out no longer. While hope remained he had resisted despair; now the resistance failed. He entered the unlit parlour beside the sickroom and stared through the dark windows, digging his nails into the wooden frame. His eyes seemed to burrow into the night seeking hope; his mind crouched as though preparing to leap towards a miracle. Then, for an instant, everything went quiet and lucid. In that lucidity he turned from the window, flung himself across a nearby table, and sobbed without a tear.

Back in the sickroom he found another convulsion underway. He stared as if trying to kill himself with the sight: tiny white fists with bluish nails, fixed eyes rolling in their sockets, the twisted mouth, teeth grinding like metal on stone. Dreadful as it was, worse followed. When the fit ended and the body softened, relaxing in the blessed easing of pain, terror crept into the little boy's eyes at the first hint that another fit was approaching. His silent appeal for rescue grew as the pain came closer and closer. To witness that and be unable to help, even with his own heart's blood, even with everything he owned! He raised clenched fists towards heaven in a threat, snatched up his child in a frantic urge to escape, then fell to his knees on the floor. He prayed to the Lord in heaven, Who holds the earth frightened through punishments and trials, Who sends poverty, illness, anguish, and death, Who requires every knee to bend trembling before Him. From Him there is no escape, neither at the ocean's farthest limits nor deep within the earth. He is the God Who, when He chooses, will crush your dearest one beneath His foot, tormenting him back into the dust from which He Himself made him.
With thoughts like these Niels Lyhne addressed his prayers to God. He cast himself before the heavenly throne in absolute surrender, admitting that all power belonged to Him alone.
The child's suffering continued.
Near dawn, as the family's old doctor finally drove through the gateway, Niels sat alone.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Autumn had arrived. No flowers remained on the graves in the churchyard, and beneath the trees of Lönborggaard the fallen leaves lay brown, rotting in the damp.

Niels Lyhne wandered the vacant rooms in bitter discouragement. The night his son died, something inside him had broken. He no longer trusted himself, no longer believed people could endure the lives given them. Existence was leaking; through every crack its substance drained away, without design or reason.

He gained nothing by calling that prayer a father's frantic appeal for his child, uttered despite knowing nobody could hear. Even at the bottom of despair he had understood his action. Temptation had overcome him; he had fallen, and the fall betrayed both himself and his ideal. Probably the inherited force within his blood had been too strong. For thousands of years humanity had called upon heaven in its anguish, and he had obeyed an ancestral impulse. Yet he should have resisted. His mind knew to its deepest fibres that gods were dreams. He had known, while praying, that he was seeking shelter inside a dream, just as in earlier years he had known the fantasies into whose arms he flung himself _were_ fantasies. Life as it stood had proved more than he could bear. He had joined the struggle for the highest things, then deserted his sworn banner under the pressure of battle. For what were the new ideal, atheism, the holy pursuit of truth? What did any of them mean beyond glittering names for one plain demand: to endure life as it was! To endure it as it was, and let it develop under its own laws!

He felt his life had finished during that terrible night. Everything since was an irrelevant scene appended to a play after its fifth act, when the action had already ended. He could resume his former convictions if he wished, certainly. But the fall had happened once; whether it ever happened again was of no consequence whatsoever.
Most often, this was the feeling that held him.
Then, one November day, the King died. War appeared increasingly close at hand.
He quickly settled matters at Lönborggaard and volunteered for military service.

He found the routine of training tolerable. Simply knowing he was no longer unnecessary felt wonderful. Once on active duty, the constant struggle with cold, lice, and every sort of hardship brought his thoughts back to immediate things, keeping them from wandering beyond what lay directly before him. He became almost light-hearted. His health, weakened by the previous year's sorrows, returned completely.
On a dark March day a bullet struck his chest.

Hjerrild, serving as a hospital doctor, arranged a bed for him in a small four-bed room. One patient had been hit in the spine and lay entirely motionless. A second, wounded in the chest, talked feverishly for hours, his words coming in short, hurried bursts. Beside Niels lay the third: a powerful young farmworker with round, fleshy cheeks. A shell fragment had struck his brain. Endlessly, hour upon hour, roughly twice a minute, he raised his right leg and right arm together, then dropped them. A loud, flat, hollow “Hah-ho!” accompanied each movement, always in precisely the same rhythm, “Hah” as the limbs rose, “ho” as they fell.
There Niels Lyhne lay, a bullet lodged in his right lung with no exit wound. Wartime allows little room for evasions; they told him his likelihood of surviving was very small.
The news astonished him. He did not feel near death, and the injury caused little pain. Soon, though, a growing weakness told him that the doctor's warning was correct.

So it ended here. Throughout the first day he kept thinking of Gerda. Yet every recollection met that unfamiliar coolness in her final look, when he last held her. How beautiful, how piercingly beautiful, if she had clung to him until the end, seeking his eyes until death clouded her own. If only she had been willing to breathe her final breath against the heart that so dearly loved her, instead of turning away at the last to secure herself further life, and still more life!

On his second hospital day the room's thick air weighed on him increasingly. The craving for fresh air became strangely entangled with the desire to remain alive. There had, after all, been much beauty in life. He remembered the clean wind along the shore at home, its cool whisper in Sjaelland's beech woods, the pure air of the mountains at Clarens, and Lake Garda's evening breezes. Thinking of people, however, sickened his soul once more. He called them before him individually; each passed and left him, none remained. But how firmly had he kept hold of them? Had he been faithful? Perhaps he had merely released his grasp more slowly. No, that was _not_ it. The bleak fact was that each soul remains alone. All faith in one soul merging with another was false. Neither the mother whose lap had held you, nor the friend, nor the wife sleeping against your heart....
By evening inflammation had begun, and the wound became more painful.
Hjerrild spent a few minutes beside him that evening, then returned at midnight for a longer vigil. Niels was in severe agony, groaning as the pain gripped him.
“Let me ask you seriously, Lyhne,” Hjerrild said. “Would you like a clergyman brought here?”
“Clergymen concern me no more than they concern you,” Niels answered in an angry whisper.

“Leave me out of it! I'm healthy and living. Don't torment yourself on that bed for the sake of your convictions. The dying have no opinions, and any they do have are irrelevant. Opinions are meant for living; they may be useful while we live, but which one we die holding makes no difference. Listen, everybody carries bright, affectionate recollections of childhood. I've watched dozens of people dying, and recalling those memories invariably comforts them. Let's admit the truth! Whatever name we give ourselves, we never quite dislodge that God from heaven. Our minds have pictured Him there too often. Bells and songs have impressed the image on us ever since we were small.”
Niels inclined his head.
Hjerrild leaned closer, ready to hear anything he might wish to say.
“You're very kind,” Niels breathed, “but”—his head moved in a firm refusal.
For a long time silence filled the ward, broken only by the farmboy's unending “Hah-ho!” pounding the hours into fragments.
Hjerrild stood. “Farewell, Lyhne. Dying for our unhappy country is, after all, an honourable way to die.”
“Yes,” Niels answered, “but this isn't how we imagined playing our part, back in those days so very long ago.”
Hjerrild went away. Back in his room, he remained at the window a long while, his gaze lifted towards the stars.
“If I were God,” he murmured. Inwardly he finished the thought: “I'd far rather grant salvation to the man who didn't convert at the final moment.”
The wound hurt more fiercely by the hour, tearing and gripping his chest without a moment's mercy. What comfort there might have been in a god to whom he could cry out and pray!
Around dawn delirium began; the inflammation was spreading quickly.
This continued through another two days and another two nights.
When Hjerrild last visited Niels Lyhne, he was talking incoherently about his armour and the need to die on his feet.
At last came his death, the difficult death.
